documents.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in education, it is important to know how confident teachers feel about using it. Research has examined AI literacy, AI readiness and AI competency, yet few validated instruments measure teachers' AI self-efficacy specifically. The aim of this study was to develop and validate the Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers (AISES-T). Methods Data were collected from teachers in different regions of Turkiye within a scale development design. Following expert review, a pool of 50 items was reduced to a 27-item trial form. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using principal axis factoring was conducted in a first sample of 313 teachers, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted in a second, independent sample of 559 teachers. Results The EFA yielded 22 items in three factors — AI Use and Learning Self-Efficacy (11 items), Pedagogical AI Integration Self-Efficacy (7 items) and AI Awareness and Understanding Self-Efficacy (4 items) — explaining 68.51% of the variance. The CFA supported the three-factor model, χ 2 (194) = 681.49, p < 0.001, χ 2 /df = 3.51, RMSEA = 0.067 (90% CI [0.062, 0.073]), SRMR = 0.044, CFI = 0.956, IFI = 0.956, TLI = 0.948, which fitted considerably better than a one-factor model, Δ χ 2 (3) = 2,202.35, p < 0.001. Cronbach's α coefficients were 0.92–0.96 for the subscales and 0.96 for the whole scale, and composite reliability ranged from 0.92 to 0.95. Standardized loadings (0.645–0.917) and average variance extracted (AVE = 0.609–0.730) supported convergent validity, while the Fornell-Larcker criterion and heterotrait-monotrait ratios (0.632–0.776) supported discriminant validity. Discussion The results show that teachers' AI self-efficacy comprises related but distinguishable beliefs about learning with AI, integrating it into instruction and understanding how it works. The AISES-T offers a valid and reliable measure for research on AI-supported teaching and for planning teacher professional development.

This Qualitative descriptive study explored how 15 in service Junior Elementary School teachers (JESTs) at Government Higher Secondary School Dad Laghari, Sindh, Pakistan, described their familiarity and use of artificial intelligence (GenAI) for lesson planning, perceived benefits and challenges, and professional learning and support needs. Participants provided written English responses to five open ended questions and profile information. Responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and participant characteristics were summarized descriptively. From the study five themes were identified like Familiarity with GenAI and reported planning uses; perceived efficiency and expanded planning options; verification of generated materials for accuracy and classroom fit; integration of AI fluency with subject and pedagogical knowledge ; and collegial and institutional support. Teachers reported using GenAI to draft lesson notes, questions, activities, examples, and explanations. Thirteen reported frequent use, while two reported occasional use. Participants showed concerns about accuracy, curriculum and learner suitability, privacy and internet access and identified need for practical training, peer exchange, digital resources and school guidance. The findings highlights self reported perspective from one school; lesson plan, classroom practice and student outcomes were not assessed.

Artificial intelligence is commonly presented as neutral, autonomous, and future-oriented, yet its interfaces, narratives, and labor infrastructures remain shaped by older gendered expectations. This article advances a new account of AI feminization by connecting symbolic representation to the material organization of hidden labor. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines interface analysis of fifteen widely used AI systems, critical discourse analysis of 500 public and industry artifacts published between 2018 and 2026, and critical infrastructural document analysis of job advertisements, contractor records, technical reports, model cards, labor documents, and workplace policies. The findings show that AI systems repeatedly perform feminized qualities such as care, patience, emotional responsiveness, availability, and service, while the labor producing these qualities is distributed across annotators, moderators, evaluators, and quality-assurance workers whose contributions remain obscured. The study further demonstrates that AI’s promises of empowerment and efficiency coexist with contractual precarity, surveillance, emotional burden, and unequal global value extraction. By theorizing AI as feminized in interface, discourse, and infrastructure, the article reveals algorithmic intelligence as a social relation rather than a technical achievement. More equitable AI futures therefore require labor visibility, accountability, worker protection, and infrastructural justice.

documents.abstract: This article examines how the progressive rollout of artificial intelligence, and prospectively artificial general intelligence (AGI), alters the equation between institutional power, human autonomy, individual agency and the democratic franchise. Treating AI as a "bureaucratic native" that realises the Weberian ideal of rule-bound, impersonal administration, it traces the shift of discretion from street-level to system-level and algorithmic bureaucracy, and then applies a PESTEL (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal) analysis. The political section argues for traceable audit trails over civic registries; the economic section offers a stylised illustration of the human labour share and contrasts Universal Basic Income with Universal Basic Capital; the social section draws on the Dutch SyRI judgment and the Rotterdam welfare-algorithm case; and the environmental and legal sections address the compute–energy trilemma, the GDPR, the EU AI Act as amended by the AI Omnibus, and Council of Europe Convention CETS No. 225. Three comparative tables and five figures summarise the argument. The article concludes that the distribution of power in the AGI epoch will be determined less by the capability of the technology than by the legal, economic and institutional choices that encode meaningful human oversight, explanation and appeal. **Keywords:** artificial general intelligence; PESTEL; algorithmic bureaucracy; artificial discretion; algorithmic due process; audit trails; labour share; Universal Basic Capital; data centres; EU AI Act; GDPR; CETS 225; KSCCN

documents.abstract: Short-form video applications are widely used worldwide. At the same time, new concerns have been raised owing to excessive and addictive short-form video use, with significant harm to health and well-being. By self-determination theory, the present study aimed to test the effects of satisfaction and frustration of three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) in relation to short-form video addiction (SVA) and evaluate the roles of the intrinsic motivations for passing time and entertainment underlying such relationships. The study included 367 Chinese TikTok users (37.1% male) aged 18 to 62 years ( M ± SD = 20.63 ± 4.40 years), who voluntarily completed an anonymous online questionnaire without compensation. All three types of need satisfaction had significant negative associations with SVA, while the three types of need frustration were significantly positively associated with SVA. Entertainment motivation significantly and negatively mediated the relationship between competence/relatedness satisfaction and SVA while significantly and positively mediating the relationship between relatedness frustration and SVA. Motivation for passing time served as a risk-enhancing mediator in the relationship between competence/relatedness frustration and SVA. Therefore, this study identified relatedness frustration and motivation for passing time as the most salient risk factors of SVA. The implications for SVA interventions that focus on psychological needs and intrinsic motivation are also discussed.

Life experiences can shape policy attitudes, but we only live one life. Citizens may therefore fail to support policies addressing risks they have never personally experienced. Narratives can make such risks immediate and personal, but personalized stories remain difficult to produce at scale. Here we ask whether AI can make distant scenarios feel concrete by simulating a participant's life as if that scenario occurred. We present the As-If Machine (AIM), a multi-agent system through which people co-write personalized counterfactual narratives---stories about their own lives under different policy futures. In two pre-registered and quota-matched experiments on science funding (N=1,007) and satellite cybersecurity (N=894), we compared AIM with two controls: reading an expert-written vignette on the same topic and co-writing with AIM about an unrelated topic. AIM increased psychological closeness---how close a risk feels to the self---by nearly identical margins in the two domains (0.36 and 0.38 standard deviations (SDs) against the vignette, 0.80 and 0.90 against unrelated writing). AIM increased psychological closeness even among participants with unfavorable views of AI. For policy attitudes, AIM's effects were 0.16 SDs against the vignette and 0.10 SDs (n.s.) against unrelated writing for science funding; the corresponding effects for satellite cybersecurity were 0.54 and 0.67 SDs. Across 23,496 human-AI autocomplete interactions, participants and the system played distinct roles: AIM supplied concrete detail that grounded the scenario, and participants supplied first-person perspective and emotion. Co-writing with the As-If Machine makes distant policy risks feel close.

Management consulting sells structured judgment: research, analysis, synthesis and recommendation, delivered under time pressure by teams organised as a pyramid of junior analysts and senior partners. Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) now performs a growing share of the pyramid's base — desk research, data analysis, benchmarking, first-draft synthesis — and is beginning to perform parts of its middle, including option generation and scenario construction. This conceptual paper asks what happens to strategic advice when the technology moves from assisting consultants to acting alongside them. Drawing on the automation–augmentation paradox, research on the changing sources of competitive advantage in AI, and the dynamic capabilities tradition, we develop a five-level maturity framework for agentic AI in consulting and strategic advice: (1) Assisted, (2) Augmented Analysis, (3) Generative Partnership, (4) Agentic Workflows, and (5) Governed Autonomous Operations. For each level we specify the AI capabilities in use, the changing human role, the principal risks, and the governance required before a firm should advance to the next level. We then propose four governance principles for AI-augmented advice — named human accountability, an explicit decision-rights ladder, evidence and audit requirements, and a protected right to override — and derive three propositions for empirical research. The framework is addressed to consulting firm leaders redesigning their leverage model, to clients learning how to buy and challenge AI-augmented advice, and to business schools whose graduates will enter a profession whose entry-level tasks are being automated first.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence has raised concerns that knowledge work may become less dependent on human-to-human interaction. Yet because AI-generated outputs require interpretation, verification, and social legitimation, generative AI may instead increase collaboration among workers. We test these competing predictions using passively collected behavioral data from more than 12,000 knowledge workers observed over 13 months during the staged organizational rollout of an AI-powered assistant (Microsoft Copilot). Using two complementary quasi-experimental designs -- a staggered difference-in-differences model and a fixed-effects instrumental-variable approach -- we estimate the effects of generative AI on workers' collaboration behavior and social network structure. We estimate that generative AI increased collaboration time across communication channels and reshaped individual networks. Those using generative AI interacted with more colleagues and their networks became less clustered, indicating broadening in collaboration structures. At the same time, they also concentrated more of their collaboration on ties with stronger prior histories, deepening reliance on already trusted colleagues. Together, these findings suggest that, while generative AI changes how people work, it may not displace human-to-human interactions.

documents.abstract: This study explores how employees experience and negotiates digital performance monitoring and algorithm-supported management in Pakistani workplaces, focusing on autonomy, privacy, fairness, and workplace trust. An exploratory qualitative design was employed, drawing on condensed summaries of semi-structured online interviews with 22 participants across diverse occupational and sectoral settings. Reflexive thematic analysis identified six interrelated themes: negotiating visibility, autonomy under metrics, privacy boundaries, supervisor-dependent fairness, organizational rules and occupational responsibilities, and employee voice and opportunities for challenge. Findings indicate that participants generally acknowledged monitoring benefits, including improved coordination, clearer performance expectations, and compliance support, while expressing concerns about inadequate contextual evaluation, behavioural pressures, unclear data practices, and limited opportunities to contest assessments. A central insight is the distinction between supportive managerial relationships and dependable organizational safeguards. Although supervisors may provide explanations and contextual consideration, employees also require transparent review authority, recognized correction procedures, clear privacy boundaries, and accessible channels for raising concerns. The study contributes an exploratory, employee-centred perspective on responsible algorithmic management and offers practical recommendations for more transparent, context-sensitive, and accountable workplace monitoring. documents.abstract: Abstract We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.

Power systems face climate-driven extremes, compound hazards, rapid electrification and renewable integration, and infrastructure decisions whose consequences persist for decades. These conditions often cannot be represented by historical patterns or well-defined probability distributions. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to forecasting, outage prediction, asset management, optimisation and resilience planning, yet most applications remain prediction-centric, whereas long-horizon grid planning takes place under deep uncertainty. This critical narrative review integrates literature from power-systems engineering, machine learning, climate-risk assessment, infrastructure resilience and decision-making under deep uncertainty to examine how AI can move from forecasting toward robust and adaptive planning. We identify a prediction–planning gap created by two mismatches: a temporal mismatch between the horizons over which AI is predictively competent and those over which infrastructure decisions operate, and an uncertainty mismatch between the stationarity assumptions of learned models and the non-stationary, deeply uncertain conditions of future grids. Distribution shift, rare extremes, model disagreement and optimisation fragility limit prediction-centric approaches. AI offers greater long-term value through scenario exploration, surrogate-accelerated simulation, stress testing, vulnerability discovery, robust multi-objective optimisation and adaptive decision support. We operationalise this shift through an AI-Enabled Adaptive Resilience Planning Framework of six iterative stages, propose a decision-performance evaluation scheme (robustness, regret, adaptability, option value, recovery, equity and tail cost), and set out eight research priorities. Next-generation grid resilience should judge AI not by how accurately it predicts one future, but by how well it supports robust, equitable, explainable and adaptable decisions across many plausible futures.

Health is one of the most fundamental human needs. Ensuring the occupational health and safety of healthcare workers is essential for the safe and effective delivery of healthcare services. This issue has been extensively addressed in graduate theses from various perspectives. To reveal the current state of literature and guide future research, this study examines graduate theses focusing on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector, in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Accordingly, 555 graduate theses completed between 1990 and 2024 were included in this study were included. The theses included in the study were examined using content analyses. The theses were classified by considering various aspects, such as year of publication, thesis type, university, department, research topic, and research method used. The findings show that most theses were at the master’s level, their number increased steadily over time, and the highest output in the last five years was in 2022. While the theses were produced at 137 different universities, the highest number was produced at Beykent University within the Institute of Health Sciences and the Department of Health Management. Studies focusing on risk assessment and management were the most predominant. The findings of this study are expected to guide and motivate research on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the relationship between humans and digital technology. Unlike digital systems that primarily delivered information, mediated interpersonal communication, or provided entertainment, generative AI can respond conversationally, personalise interactions, produce immediate solutions, simulate empathy, reduce cognitive effort, and remain continuously available. These characteristics raise an emerging question: can repeated engagement with generative AI develop into psychologically dependent or addiction-like patterns, and, if so, through what mechanisms? This paper employs an integrative critical literature review and conceptual synthesis to examine problematic generative-AI use through the combined perspectives of behavioural addiction theory, reward and reinforcement processes, the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) model, self-determination theory, compensatory technology use, social anxiety, loneliness, anthropomorphism, cognitive offloading, and human psychological needs. The current study identifies a major gap in the current literature: emerging research frequently examines AI dependence as either a behavioural outcome, an educational problem, or a form of social attachment, but insufficiently integrates the neuropsychological processes of reinforcement with the psychological needs that make generative AI personally rewarding. To address this gap, this paper proposes the Need–Reward–Dependence (NRD) Framework, according to which problematic GenAI engagement develops through the interaction of three processes: unmet or salient psychological needs, rapid need-contingent reinforcement delivered by AI, and repeated cognitive or emotional outsourcing that strengthens habitual reliance. The framework proposes that competence, relatedness, autonomy, reassurance, emotional regulation, cognitive ease, social safety, and control can act as psychologically rewarding affordances of generative AI. Repeated reinforcement may increase cue-reactivity, habitual checking, perceived indispensability, cognitive delegation, emotional attachment, and impaired self-regulation in susceptible users. Importantly, this paper does not claim that generative-AI addiction is currently established as a distinct psychiatric disorder. Rather, it argues that a theoretically coherent and increasingly empirically observable continuum exists from adaptive use through reliance and dependence to potentially compulsive engagement associated with functional impairment. The paper concludes that future research should distinguish productive high-frequency use from clinically meaningful problematic use and should examine the interaction between users’ psychological vulnerabilities and the reward architecture of generative-AI systems

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address a gap in contemporary scholarship on generative artificial intelligence (AI) by shifting attention from the functional evaluation of AI systems to the formative impact of repeated AI use on the human user. It introduces formative evaluation as a complementary approach concerned with how sustained AI use may shape cognitive skills, habits, reasoning, judgment and agency over time. To address this concern, the paper proposes the REAL Framework (Retained, Eroded, Atrophied, Leveraged) as a practical means of evaluating and intentionally shaping patterns of AI use. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper develops the REAL Framework through interdisciplinary synthesis and theoretical analysis. It integrates scholarship on human agency and principal-agent relationships with research on cognitive offloading, cognitive reserve, desirable difficulty, automation bias and human–AI collaboration. Emerging empirical research on the cognitive effects of generative AI is used to contextualize and support the framework. The resulting four-dimensional framework is then illustrated through its application to professional practice and considered in relation to potential objections, limitations and directions for future empirical research. Findings The analysis identifies formative evaluation as a distinct and underdeveloped dimension of AI evaluation. While emerging research increasingly documents potential cognitive effects of generative AI use, practical means of evaluating and responding to those effects remain limited. The REAL Framework addresses this gap through four dimensions: Retained, Eroded, Atrophied and Leveraged. Together, these dimensions distinguish between AI use that preserves human agency and cognitive engagement, use that risks over-delegation and capability loss, and use that intentionally leverages AI to enhance human thinking and judgment. Research limitations/implications The REAL Framework is a conceptual and reflective framework that has not yet been empirically validated or operationalized as a measurement instrument. Longitudinal research is needed to examine the formative effects of sustained generative AI use and determine whether structured application of the framework influences patterns of AI delegation or preserves cognitive engagement and capability. Future research should develop and test measures associated with the framework’s four dimensions and examine their applicability across educational, professional and organizational contexts. Practical implications The REAL Framework provides individuals and institutions with a practical means of evaluating how generative AI is being incorporated into learning and professional practice. Its four reflective dimensions can help users identify inappropriate over-delegation, preserve important cognitive and professional capabilities, and redesign AI use to support rather than replace human reasoning and judgment. The framework may also inform institutional guidance, professional development and AI literacy initiatives by shifting attention from whether AI should be used toward how it can be used while preserving meaningful human agency and engagement. Social implications As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in education, work and everyday decision-making, its societal effects will depend not only on the capabilities of AI systems but also on how their use shapes human capabilities over time. The REAL Framework highlights the importance of preserving human agency, reasoning, judgment and cognitive engagement while benefiting from technological advancement. It encourages a broader societal conversation about which human capacities should remain meaningfully exercised and which may appropriately be delegated to increasingly capable AI systems. Originality/value This paper introduces formative evaluation as a distinct conceptual approach to understanding generative AI use, complementing prevailing functional approaches concerned primarily with AI systems, governance and responsible use. It advances the REAL Framework as a structured means of translating emerging concerns about AI’s cognitive and formative effects into reflective practice. By connecting human agency and delegation with cognitive development, the framework shifts attention from evaluating what AI can do to evaluating what repeated AI use may be doing to the human user.

documents.abstract: Abstract Sociologists face the pressing question of how large language model-based technologies can contribute to social theorising. Several social scientists have called for a greater integration of generative AI tools in the social sciences and humanities to speed and scale up the production of social theory. In this article, we adopt a more cautious approach, reflecting on how the adoption of generative AI raises foundational questions about the construction, refinement and evaluation of critical social theory. To make this argument, we create and critically analyse a speculative piece of dystopian sociological fiction. This enables us to explore the values and practices of critical social theory authorship. We argue that authorship must be ‘recentred’, particularly with regard to four key values of authorial practice: (1) standpoint, (2) creativity, (3) pluralism and (4) accountability. In the present moment, the use of generative AI as substitution for authorial practices redefines and potentially threatens authorship in ways that problematises its particular use in generating critical social theory. With regards to standpoint, generative AI technologies run the risk of reproducing an ‘abstract masculinity’ that feminist scholars have long written against. The relational wonder at the heart of social theory creativity is undermined by generative AI use, as is the pluralism of creativity. Generative AI also flattens and overlooks pluralism of voice, as well as dilutes authorial accountability. We sociologists need to defend and rearticulate what we contribute to social theory and its concomitant politics, both in the theories themselves and in the project of social theorising. It is with this in mind that we call for the ‘rebirth’ - that is, the recentralisation - of the human author in critical social theory creation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the periphery of experimental computing to the centre of managerial practice, reshaping how organisations make decisions, allocate resources, engage customers and manage people. Despite the rapid growth of scholarship on the subject, the literature remains fragmented across functional silos, and the opportunities and risks of AI are frequently examined in isolation from one another. This conceptual study synthesises existing literature to examine the role of AI in modern business management and to articulate an integrated understanding of its opportunities and challenges. Drawing on the technology–organisation–environment framework, the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory and the automation–augmentation perspective, the paper develops a conceptual model comprising five interrelated components: AI adoption enablers, AI applications across management functions, the dual effects of AI (opportunities and challenges), organisational outcomes, and moderating governance mechanisms. The model proposes that AI generates sustainable value only when technological capability is matched by organisational readiness, responsible governance, effective human–AI collaboration and continuous workforce development. The discussion elaborates the implications of the model for strategic decision-making, operations, marketing, human resource management and finance, and considers the ethical, social and implementation challenges that accompany adoption. The paper contributes a theoretically grounded and integrative framework that can guide future empirical research and support managers who seek to adopt AI responsibly and effectively.

documents.abstract: Abstract The "Provisional specification.pdf" introduces a comprehensive security architecture for governing autonomous artificial intelligence agents across isolated runtimes, administrative domains, and hardware environments. As AI agents increasingly invoke external tools and modify persistent data, the system distinguishes between an agent's ability to compute and its authority to execute consequential external effects. The architecture intercepts proposed agent operations, holding them in a non-effective state while a protected enforcement domain evaluates operation-specific authorization conditions and commits validation evidence. A scoped, non-bearer finality capability is then verified at an effectuation sink before the operation can produce real-world consequences. The specification covers advanced technical mechanisms including micro-virtual-machine isolation, task-preserving context minimization, distributed revocation, and hardware-level command accounting. Why You Should Download This Document You should download this specification if you are building, securing, or deploying autonomous AI agents that interact with enterprise resources, financial systems, or cloud infrastructure. It provides a detailed blueprint for preventing unauthorized external actions caused by prompt injection, compromised models, or hallucinated tool invocations. The document offers actionable implementations for deploying agents within virtual machines, micro-virtual machines, and OS-level containers while maintaining strict cryptographic and hardware-assisted oversight over API requests, network egress, and persistent memory mutations. Industry-Relevant Keywords Artificial-Intelligence-Agent Sandboxing Protected Execution-Finality Architecture Non-Effective State (NES) Staging Scoped Non-Bearer Finality Capability Cryptographically Isolated Enforcement Domain (CIED) Micro-Virtual-Machine (Micro-VM) Isolation Transitive Effect-Closure Admission Autonomous Guardian Supervision Alignment with Industry Direction (Meta Muse & NVIDIA) The architecture detailed in the provisional specification strongly aligns with the current trajectory of consumer and enterprise AI agent platforms. Meta's newly launched Muse agent runs in isolated, secure virtual machines on the cloud to execute multi-step tasks across connected applications while attempting to limit unintended access to user credentials and ad systems. The specification provides a formalized, enterprise-grade extension of this concept, detailing how to implement micro-virtual-machine isolation and lifecycle-bound authority so that an agent's access to a tool connector does not automatically grant unrestricted execution rights. Similarly, as NVIDIA scales its AI hardware and NIM microservices for agentic workflows, the specification’s coverage of hardware-resident effect-budget accounting, accelerator-memory sanitization, and hardware queue containment offers a precise technical framework for securing agent workloads at the GPU and DPU layer

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity. As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes. This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domain-specific findings. The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality. Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control. Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority. Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems. Domain-specific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.

With artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influencing children’s and youth’s lives, AI literacy has been promoted as an educational concern at all levels of schooling. While AI literacy initiatives are being introduced globally, the specific components and the objectives of this literacy remain undecided. This position paper challenges the current discourse of AI literacy by drawing attention to multiple purposes of AI literacy in middle school education that may co-exist and collide. We do so by applying Biesta’s world-centred education framework as an analytical lens, and by grounding the argument in classroom observations and interviews with middle school students. Our findings highlight both tensions and overlaps between middle school students’ often vague and fragmented formal knowledge and skills (qualification) of what AI is and how it works, and their more developed reflections related to norms and ethical concerns (socialisation), as well as agency (subjectification). We suggest that for AI literacy to truly empower students, both curriculum design and professional development must account for a broad spectrum of educational goals.

Justification: Deficiencies in proportional reasoning with which students enter higher education affect the understanding of more complex content; therefore, pedagogical strategies are required to help overcome these difficulties. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of artificial intelligence–based tutoring in strengthening proportional reasoning among first-semester students at a public university in the province of Manabí, Ecuador. Methodology: A quantitative approach with a descriptive-comparative scope was adopted, using a pre-experimental pretest–posttest design with two groups. The sample consisted of 78 students. The intervention involved tutoring supported by artificial intelligence tools, structured in two stages: prior knowledge construction and proportional problem solving. Data were collected using two performance tests designed to assess the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships. Results: After the pedagogical intervention, the results showed a shift toward higher performance levels in both groups, with a reduction in the low level and a significant increase in the high level. Specifically, improvements were observed in the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships; however, the change in identification was less pronounced. Inferential analyses revealed statistically significant differences between the pretest and posttest (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Conclusion: Artificial intelligence–based tutoring strengthened proportional reasoning among the first-semester students who participated in this study.

documents.abstract: Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints and watching every drone. We present UAV SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a vision-language model, splits them among N UAVs by balancing route length, and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3 foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law. The second UAV delivers half of the attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52x. We discuss what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.

Purpose This study aims to examine the determinants of student satisfaction with their experience of using artificial intelligence (AI) tools for learning-related activities in Vietnamese higher education, addressing a gap in research that has focused primarily on AI adoption and usage, with limited …

Purpose As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life and workplace operations, research has begun to document numerous organizational benefits, including enhanced efficiency and productivity. However, employees’ personal experiences with AI and how these experiences spill over into the work domain remain underexplored. Using sociomateriality as a sensitizing lens, we propose and test a sequential process in which personal AI use increases work-related AI use, further enhancing employees’ psychological capital, ultimately improving their service innovation performance. We further examine conscientiousness as an important boundary condition that moderates this pathway. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 uses a three-wave survey of 438 service employees and employs structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized serial mediation. Study 2 extends this investigation by examining within-person dynamics using a daily experience sampling design with 121 participants and testing the moderating role of conscientiousness. Findings Across both studies, personal AI use positively predicts employees’ work-related AI use, which in turn increases their psychological capital and subsequently service innovation performance. Moreover, employees lower in conscientiousness benefit more from AI use. Originality/value This paper contributes to our understanding of personal AI use’s spillover effect in the work domain, suggesting AI use may introduce psychological affordances that were less evident in earlier technologies. Our research demonstrates that individual personality differences can influence the effectiveness of human–AI collaboration.

As artificial intelligence systems become more capable, their behavior may become increasingly difficult to predict. This article examines whether behavioral unpredictability necessarily undermines the ability to govern consequential AI actions. It argues that uncertainty about what a system may propose does not, by itself, defeat action-specific pre-execution authorization. The analysis distinguishes three separate properties: predicting a system's behavior, determining whether a proposed action is permitted under applicable policy and authority, and enforcing that determination before execution. It challenges the assumption that assigning a second, equally or more intelligent AI system to supervise the first resolves the governance problem. Collusion, common-mode failures, and recursive supervision raise questions that additional intelligence alone cannot settle. It separates standing eligibility from runtime authorization: a test-then-trust regime releases on a prior assessment and is exactly as vulnerable to concealed capability as its critics say, while action-specific authorization gates each consequential action under the policy in force at execution. And it distinguishes the authorization requirement, which does not change as capability grows, from the deployment-specific evidence that a boundary remains complete and independent, which must remain valid under the capability model actually in scope. The article develops a three-part analytical framework distinguishing evaluation independence, authority independence, and enforcement independence. It explains why independently derived evaluations do not automatically confer permission, why intelligent supervisors may exercise legitimately delegated authority without becoming an alternative execution path, and why consequential release must remain dependent on an independently enforced authorization verdict. The central architectural argument is conditional. Enforceable authorization requires demonstrated coverage of governed effect-bearing execution paths, protection of the enforcement mechanism against unauthorized control, adequate governing inputs, and valid authority. A boundary-emitted ALLOW permits release; DENY and unresolved ABSTAIN prevent execution. A tamper-evident authorization artifact supports independent reconstruction of the verdict, while separate execution-path evidence is needed to establish that release actually depended on that verdict. The article also examines the limits of this approach, including compromised supervisory determinations, defective authorization inputs, improperly established policy authority, unauthorized AI proliferation outside governed environments, and harmful outcomes from legitimately authorized actions. It does not claim that authorization guarantees safe behavior or universal AI containment. Central conclusion: Behavioral unpredictability does not remove the requirement for enforceable permission over consequential actions. Unpredictability is not permission. Scope A doctrine article in the FERZ AI Governance Corpus. Its claims are analytical and conditional; it asserts no implementation-specific capability and describes no FERZ product. The canonical publication is the ferz.ai page: ferz.ai/articles/unpredictable-intelligence-still-requires-authorization. This record is the citable version of record for the edition. documents.abstract: Abstract Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human–model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor’s capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how people seek information, yet communicating AI factuality to laypeople remains challenging. Through a mixed-methods investigation involving interviews (N=8), a survey (N=1,000), and an experiment (N=5,151), we examine how people evaluate AI-generated information for gardening, mathematical, and medical queries, and how factuality indicators (confidence and sources) shape perceptions. Our interviews and survey show people selectively verify AI responses using external and AI-provided evidence, moderated by contextual factors. Although confidence-indicators affected trust and accuracy perceptions, people hold diverse, ambiguous interpretations of AI confidence. Sources were viewed as crucial, yet users raised concerns about source reliability and verification effort. Our experiment showed that confidence and source-based indicators influenced initial perceptions, but effects disappeared once participants learned the response's correctness. Medical queries elicited skepticism regardless of indicator. Findings motivate helping users interpret model confidence and integrating source information into the interface to support calibrated trust in AI-supported information-seeking.

documents.abstract: This cross-sectional quantitative research aimed to study the level of motivation and factors associated with participation in professional development training among personnel at Sansai Hospital, Chiang Mai Province. The sample consisted of 200 personnel at Sansai Hospital, selected through stratified random sampling by mission groups. Data were collected using a questionnaire validated for content validity (IOC > 0.8) and reliability (α = 0.75). Data analysis employed descriptive statistics, comparative tests, and binary logistic regression analysis. Results showed that personnel had an overall high level of motivation (x̄ = 3.95, SD = 0.84), with intrinsic motivation higher than extrinsic motivation (x̄ = 4.21 and 3.68, respectively). Factors significantly associated with training participation decision (p < 0.05) included: self-development (adjusted OR = 2.321, 95% CI = 1.325-4.066), nursing mission group (adjusted OR = 2.440, 95% CI = 1.188-5.012), organizational support (adjusted OR = 2.125, 95% CI = 1.185-3.810), commitment and work inspiration (adjusted OR = 1.874, 95% CI = 1.096-3.204), and years of service (adjusted OR = 0.918, 95% CI = 0.859-0.981). These findings can be applied to develop personnel training policies by emphasizing intrinsic motivation enhancement, increasing organizational support, and reducing barriers to training participation.

documents.abstract: Use of internet-based technologies (IBTs) and artificial intelligence (AI) via eHealth could enhance mental healthcare delivery and accessibility. However, ethical concerns, perceptions of AI capabilities, past experience, and individual differences can influence acceptance and engagement. We qualitatively explored attitudes and behaviours toward IBTs, AI and eHealth, given the overlapping nature of these digital environments, trust, and the possible role of mental health. This exploratory study conducted semi-structured interviews between March and October 2023 with 22 UK-based participants: eight with lived experience of a mental health problem and 14 without. There was no clear difference in participants’ levels of trust in IBTs across mental health status. Participants reported using IBTs despite privacy concerns. Trust was influenced by perceptions of developer trustworthiness, individual traits, and affective responses to IBTs. Convenience, ease of use, and lack of alternatives often outweighed concerns, driving engagement. Our findings highlight that in this group trust is a key factor in IBT and eHealth uptake, but not the sole determinant, highlighting ethical concerns and responsibilities for both UK healthcare providers and developers. There is a need for transparent, ethically grounded, value-sensitive design and implementation of IBTs and AI-enabled eHealth tools that supports genuine user choice, voluntary engagement, and human interaction.

Generative artificial intelligence gives college students new ways to support their learning, while also raising questions about what they still want to learn and do for themselves. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 undergraduates at a Northeastern liberal arts college to examine how students distinguish between AI use that supports their own thinking and AI use that substitutes for it, what they believe is worth doing on their own, and whether and how purpose enters their reasoning about learning and AI use. Using the Framework Method with a cross-case matrix to compare patterns across participants and topics, we found that students repeatedly drew a line between using AI as a supportive tool and letting it take the place of their own thinking or authorship. Students most often talked about wanting to keep developing their own skills, thinking independently, and knowing what they could actually do without AI. They also wanted the work to still feel “like theirs,” citing ownership, pride, authenticity, and ethical concerns. Students also described pressures that made AI appealing, including heavy workloads, deadlines, grades, convenience, and concerns about falling behind their peers. Although few participants explicitly connected their AI choices to a stated purpose, many described concerns that may be relevant to purpose development, including developing valued skills and strengths, acting on personal values, and becoming the kind of person they hoped to be. We consider these concerns through a purpose-mindset framework while distinguishing our interpretation from participants’ own explanations of their AI choices. The findings suggest that understanding students’ AI use requires attention to what they believe they need to learn and do for themselves.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing personalized and adaptive education. Existing research has examined Human–AI hybrid adaptivity and coordination between human participants and AI systems, but clearer conceptualization is needed of the pedagogical coordination of functionally different forms of instructional support, particularly in highly abstract domains such as mathematics. This study proposes a Human–AI Orchestration Framework integrating Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs), Generative AI, and direct teacher support while retaining pedagogical orchestration and responsibility with the teacher. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, the Framework proposes Cognitive Load Redistribution as a theoretical proposition and introduces coordination mechanisms, including Handover Points and a Meta-Prompt. Its practical implementation was explored through an exploratory design pilot with 32 Grade 8 students in an authentic classroom, using observations and feedback to iteratively refine its configuration. The pilot informed several design refinements, including refinement of the Meta-Prompt, introduction of “Call the Teacher,” and adaptation of interaction formats. These formative observations provide preliminary indications of the practical feasibility of coordinating functionally different and potentially complementary forms of instructional support, while the Framework’s educational effectiveness and proposed conceptual mechanisms remain to be systematically evaluated in future research.

Abstract The European Law Institute’s Guiding Principles and Model Rules on Digital Assistants for Consumer Contracts (DACC) propose a right for consumers to use digital assistants in business-to-consumer relations. The DACC’s definition encompasses consumer AI agents (CAIAs), which use AI-generated outputs to determine transactionally relevant matters left open by consumers and initiate or perform transactional actions. The article examines two concerns. First, recognition and safeguards may create a regulatory safety halo, causing consumers to overestimate CAIAs’ technical reliability and the effectiveness of remedies for unwanted outcomes. Second, recognition may accelerate agentic markets, disproportionately benefit incumbents in adjacent digital markets, and foster concentration, to which the DMA and EU competition law provide only partial responses. Legislation should therefore first establish essential rules governing delegation, responsibility and market contestability. Technical implementation may be entrusted to European standardisation bodies, but the Commission’s request should define tasks precisely and maximise transparency and balanced stakeholder participation to mitigate legitimacy concerns. Only once CAIAs are sufficiently reliable and the legal framework more mature should the right to use a CAIA be recognised.

Purpose: This paper examines the socio-technical limitations of using artificial intelligence (AI) to modernize legacy information systems in the public sector, where continuity of services, policy obligations, security, and public accountability shape technology decisions. Design/methodology/approach: The paper combines a review of literature on public-sector AI adoption and legacy-system modernization with an anonymous survey of more than 50 public-sector technology professionals. Participants represented technical, analytical, management, application-support, and project roles and a range of professional experience. Survey topics included AI benefits and risks, organizational readiness, security and privacy, governance, workforce challenges, and human oversight. Findings: Respondents recognized AI's potential to support modernization but raised concerns about citizen-data protection, compliance, trust in generated outputs, integration, workforce readiness, and accountability. The findings suggest that AI should augment, not replace, experienced professionals and established engineering controls. Survey responses also point to the importance of governance, training, secure environments, phased implementation, and human validation. Originality: The paper brings technical, organizational, institutional, and ethical constraints together in a public-sector legacy-modernization context. It emphasizes that AI should augment, rather than replace, accountable human expertise and that successful adoption depends on governance, secure data practices, validation, and organizational readiness. Research limitations/implications: The survey reflects the views of its participants and should not be treated as representative of all public-sector technology professionals. Environmental impacts were not directly measured in the structured survey. Further research could test these findings across agencies and modernization projects.

documents.abstract: The success of recent Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has been accompanied by the opacity of their internal mechanisms, due notably to the use of deep neural networks. In order to understand these internal mechanisms and explain the output of these AI models, a set of methods have been proposed, grouped under the domain of eXplainable AI (XAI). This paper focuses on a sub-domain of XAI, called eXplainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL), which aims to explain the actions of an agent that has learned by reinforcement learning. We propose an intuitive taxonomy based on two questions ‘What’ and ‘How’. The first question focuses on the target that the method explains, while the second relates to the way the explanation is provided. We use this taxonomy to provide a state-of-the-art review of over 250 papers. In addition, we present a set of domains close to XRL, which we believe should get attention from the community. Finally, we identify some needs for the field of XRL.

Abstract Computational Thinking (CT) is increasingly expected across curricula, yet pre-service teachers often report limited preparation for translating CT concepts into instructional practice. This systematic literature review examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) supports pre-service teachers’ instructional design and what the available evidence implies for CT-oriented teaching. Using the PRISMA approach, the review synthesised 26 empirical studies identified through Scopus and ScienceDirect under the original eligibility criteria. The evidence base was heterogeneous: only two studies were coded as explicitly addressing CT integration, fifteen as implicitly CT-aligned, and nine as having no identifiable CT integration. Accordingly, indirect studies are treated as contextual evidence rather than direct evidence of CT instructional design. Across the literature, GenAI was used for ideation, lesson planning, feedback, multimedia generation, and iterative refinement. Several studies reported gains or positive experiences in efficiency, confidence, engagement, creativity, or instructional design competence; however, these outcomes were study-specific and should not be generalised as improvements in CT competence. Several studies have linked more productive use of GenAI to human evaluation, AI literacy, pedagogical or subject-matter knowledge, and structured frameworks or training. Reported risks included inaccurate or inconsistent outputs, hallucinations, overreliance, metacognitive laziness, and ethical concerns. Because the search was limited to Scopus and ScienceDirect and applied an open-access criterion, the review may be affected by database and accessibility bias. Overall, direct evidence that GenAI improves CT-specific instructional design remains preliminary; the broader literature more strongly supports a conditional role for GenAI as a pedagogical scaffold in CT-relevant instructional design.

documents.abstract: Agents can create rich representations, yet these representations are rarely used as a medium for expressing user intent. We present Agent-Bound UI, an interaction model that separates reusable interaction structures from task-specific meanings. Agents bind task-specific meanings to interactions in reusable views and publish the resulting bindings as shared state, enabling humans and agents to understand and act on shared surfaces whose meanings vary across tasks. We implement ABRA, a framework-agnostic prototype of Agent-Bound UI, in which users and agents collaborate through chat and shared interactive canvases. We demonstrate ABRA through a representative use case and evaluate four LLM-backed agents on canvas authoring, owner-side consequence resolution, and cross-agent invocation. The code and demo video are available at https://github.com/megagonlabs/abra.

AI assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are trained on human feedback and increasingly personalized to users' stated preferences. Yet how closely these preferences reflect what people reward in responses remains unclear. We compare stated and revealed preferences in the public PRISM dataset, in which 1,396 participants reported how much seven response attributes mattered to them and then rated 29,347 responses from 21 LLMs. Among responses to the same prompt, features the survey never asked about, such as response length, formatting and refusal language, were at least as strongly associated with ratings as text proxies of the surveyed attributes. Whether stated priorities matched ratings depended on how attributes were measured: participants who prioritized an attribute favoured responses from models that others perceived as strong on it, but not responses that scored higher on text proxies for it. Written feedback was more telling: participants who asked for shorter answers, even in earlier conversations, gave length less weight in their ratings, and those asking for longer answers gave it more. Their relative priorities over the surveyed attributes, however, did not predict this weight. Reasons given for choices reflected perceived attributes more than measured features. Participants also differed stably in how much they weighted several concrete features, especially length, but with a median of 6 conversations per participant, these weights were estimated poorly. The largest gain from personal information in predicting held-out choices was 0.13 percentage points, compared with 1.11 for a stronger pooled model. Stated priorities thus track perceived attributes of AI responses but say little about the concrete features that ratings reward, a distinction that matters for preference elicitation and AI personalization.

Abstract This study examines how learning agility and change self-efficacy are associated with human capital readiness through adaptive performance and whether digital readiness and organizational resilience condition these relationships. Using a quantitative explanatory design, cross-sectional survey data from 350 professional workers across government, state-owned enterprises, banking, higher education, and digital-based private organizations in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, were analyzed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Learning agility (β = 0.186, p = 0.004) and change self-efficacy (β = 0.301, p < 0.001) were positively associated with adaptive performance, while adaptive performance was positively associated with human capital readiness (β = 0.498, p < 0.001). The model explained 74.6% of the variance in adaptive performance and 73.4% in human capital readiness. Digital readiness did not significantly moderate either capability-performance relationship. Organizational resilience strengthened the learning agility-adaptive performance relationship (β = 0.135, p = 0.010) but weakened the change self-efficacy-adaptive performance relationship (β = -0.196, p = 0.016). These findings position adaptive performance as a central behavioral pathway through which individual capabilities relate to workforce readiness and show that organizational context operates asymmetrically rather than uniformly. Organizations should pair digital investment with learning-oriented work design, confidence-building support, managerial flexibility, and knowledge-sharing mechanisms. Instructors looking to support personalized mathematics learning may provide access to generative AI tutoring tools. Few studies explore the effectiveness of these systems in classroom settings. This is particularly important in mathematics, where genAI is a shift from historic adaptive intelligent tutoring systems. We evaluated undergraduate algebra students’ (n=58) use of the Socratic generative AI tutor, Khanmigo, through a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study using survey, registrar, grades, and software usage data. One course section was assigned four Khanmigo activities throughout the semester (experimental), while the other was provided access and an introductory activity only (control). A Wilcoxon Rank Sum test showed that experimental students engaged in significantly more chats than control students (p<0.05), controlling for in-class activities. Instrumental help seeking was positively correlated with Khanmigo use, while intentions of seeking help from technology sources were negatively correlated with use. Khanmigo use did significantly predict mathematics grades after controlling for prior GPA and course section. Most students reported using Khanmigo for homework help and exam prep, though lack of visuals and the Socratic design limited perceived usefulness for some students. Integrating genAI tutoring systems into class activities and setting student expectations may improve the likelihood of students using them effectively for learning.

documents.abstract: LLM agents can evolve by learning from accumulated experience. Existing approaches extract reusable external knowledge, such as skills and memories, from experience to guide subsequent task solving, with some further internalizing this knowledge through model training. However, different ways of analyzing and transforming the same experience can yield knowledge with substantially different utility, even when the resulting guidance appears reasonable. Inspired by consistency regularization, we identify consistent utility gains across different ways of analyzing the same experience, rather than relying on any single way of analyzing it. We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized knowledge-model co-evolution. It constructs evolution views by perturbing how the same experience is analyzed, producing different knowledge candidates. Knowledge updates are then guided by common gain, which accounts for utility gains and their consistency across views. During model evolution, self-distillation internalizes the evolved knowledge alongside reinforcement learning, using knowledge associated with consistent utility degradation as a contrastive reference. The two processes interleave, with model updates driving further knowledge evolution. Experiments across diverse domains show that SPLICE outperforms knowledge evolution and model training baselines by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points in average accuracy, while its evolved knowledge reduces output tokens per correct solution by up to 44% and transfers across model sizes and families.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) gradually enters the teaching and research contexts of higher education institutions, university teachers’ different perceptions of AI may elicit different psychological responses. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources model, this study examines the effects of AI Challenge Awareness and AI Threat Awareness on university teachers’ Work Stress, and further analyzes the moderating roles of Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support. Using university teachers as the research subjects, 421 valid samples were obtained through a questionnaire survey, and hierarchical regression analysis was employed to test the research hypotheses. The results indicate that AI Challenge Awareness is significantly and negatively correlated with university teachers’ Work Stress, whereas AI Threat Awareness is significantly and positively correlated with Work Stress. Both Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support significantly weaken the positive effect of AI Threat Awareness on Work Stress, but neither of their moderating effects on the relationship between AI Challenge Awareness and Work Stress reaches a significant level. The findings suggest that university teachers’ perceptions of AI do not merely manifest as a source of stress; rather, their effects depend on individuals’ different interpretations of the work-related changes brought about by AI. Compared with challenge-oriented perceptions, threat-oriented perceptions are more readily transformed into Work Stress, while Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support can, to a certain extent, buffer the stress induced by threat-oriented perceptions. The conclusions of this study help to deepen the understanding of individual differences in university teachers’ psychological responses in the context of AI, and provide references for higher education institutions to optimize the AI application environment and improve teacher support measures.

Abstract: Factchecking is among the key mechanisms for addressing information disorder. In the context of the growing integration of artificial intelligence, particularly large language models, into the information environment, the need for reliable information is increasing while access to it is more challenging. Thus, generative artificial intelligence can be both – an asset and a risk to factcheckers. The present study aims to examine the extent to which Claude.ai and ChatGPT can factcheck claims in Bulgarian. The experiment was conducted using a free skill developed by Nauka.bg. The claims were selected from the “Verified” section of Factcheck.bg, the largest fact-checking platform in Bulgaria. Through comparative content analysis, the study found that in most cases both models correctly identify false claims in accordance with Factcheck.bg’s publications. Claude.ai demonstrates a more authoritative tone and provides concise explanations supporting its verdicts. ChatGPT is more hesitant but offers greater detail, precision, and clarity in its explanations. Notably, ChatGPT rarely references its sources, whereas Claude.ai occasionally links to unreliable sources. A positive trend is Claude.ai’s note to consult official factchecking organizations and verified information sources.The results confirm the hypothesis that artificial intelligence can assist factcheckers but cannot replace human expertise in the verification process. Keywords: disinformation, factchecking, artificial intelligence, large language models, ChatGPT, Claude.ai.

Now artificial intelligence (AI) is being used can be used to help with a number of these steps. documents.abstract: A system does not have to remove choice in order to shape it. It can define the problem, structure the options that appear, and create conditions under which a voluntary choice becomes costly to reverse. These mechanisms predate artificial intelligence. This paper asks what changes when AI-mediated systems operate them at greater speed, scale, and adaptability, and when the people subject to them cannot practically inspect, contest, or leave. The paper develops a four-part lens (problem definition, choice architecture, dependency formation, reversibility) and distinguishes institutional dependency from epistemic dependency. It adds an agency and accountability audit of six questions: who sets the objective, who controls the data, model and infrastructure, who can inspect the evidence, who bears the cost of error, who can override or replace the system, and what alternatives remain. Its central hypothesis, an accountability asymmetry, is stated with the evidence that would weaken it. A rubric scores safeguards by whether they have been exercised, not merely documented, and is applied to three current arrangements: the Robodebt scheme, the Medicare WISeR model, and the UnitedHealth nH Predict litigation. Where public evidence allows no score, the gap is reported as a finding. Appendices provide a one-page citizen audit card and a legal and case status snapshot as of 21 October 2026. This is a working paper. It has not been peer reviewed and is not legal advice. Claims are labelled documented, reported, interpretation, or hypothesis. The rubric is unvalidated and was scored by a single rater from public sources. Companion to Johnson (2026a) and Johnson (2026b).

documents.abstract: Introduction Positive and negative attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) may have partly distinct psychological correlates. This cross-sectional study examined whether AI anxiety statistically accounted for associations between AI literacy and positive and negative attitudes toward AI among preservice teachers. Methods Participants were 335 preservice teachers enrolled in a faculty of education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale, and a personal information form. Two indirect-effect models were estimated using PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for prior AI training. Results AI literacy was negatively associated with AI anxiety and positively associated with positive attitudes toward AI. AI anxiety was positively associated with negative attitudes but was not significantly associated with positive attitudes. The indirect association through AI anxiety was significant for negative attitudes but not for positive attitudes, and a direct bootstrap contrast confirmed that the two indirect effects differed significantly (B = −0.118, 95% CI [−0.201, −0.039]). Prior AI training was not significantly associated with either attitude dimension. A sensitivity analysis excluding the three reverse-worded AI literacy items reproduced this pattern. Discussion The findings indicate that positive and negative attitudes toward AI may have partly distinct psychological correlates: AI literacy is directly related to positive evaluations, whereas its association with negative evaluations is statistically linked to AI anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional, the indirect effects should not be interpreted as evidence of causal mediation.

This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be integrated into business training and development (T&D) to strengthen organizational capacity for long-term viability. Drawing on action learning, experiential learning, and enterprise education, it outlines how AI-enabled tools, such as intelligent coaching systems, adaptive feedback mechanisms, and decision-support platforms, can support the development of transversal capabilities, including systemic thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making. The analysis adopts a design perspective, advancing an architecture for AI-augmented training that connects educational and workplace contexts. Strategic considerations are proposed for creating individualized and scalable learning environments that address the dual imperative of workforce development and organizational adaptability under complex, evolving conditions. The chapter integrates pedagogical models and systems design principles to offer a coherent framework for embedding AI in organizational T&D.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a nascent technology that could become a general-purpose technology and can have significant impacts on economic development, productivity growth, labour markets and good governance. The study will delve into the potential impact of Artificial Intelligence on the economy and job landscape of India as part of the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047. The study uses qualitative review-based research methodology that is based on analyzing evidence from the academic literature, government documents, as well as reports produced by national and international institutions. AI has the potential to augment productivity, innovate solutions, modernize industries, contribute to digital governance and create job opportunities, as revealed by this study. At the same time, the implementation of AI can be challenging due to the changes in labor markets, lack of skills, digital divide, fragility of the informal sector, data privacy and security concerns, algorithmic biases, and institutional preparedness. In this study, it is argued that AI will not necessarily take the place of jobs, but rather change the employment type if suitable reskilling measures are taken. It identifies the following policy priorities – human capital, digital infrastructure, responsible AI governance, research and innovation, and social protection.

documents.abstract: Accelerated progress in digital technologies has influenced all industries. Interest in embracing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education and research is flourishing among scholars, practitioners, educators, students, and the general public. Educational institutions now need to transform their traditional approach towards teaching and research by implementing innovative technologies. However, controversies surrounding the use of AI in education or research require deeper examination. Moreover, integration sustainability in business education has become an obligation for universities around the world. The significance of universities in empowering generations to tackle complex sustainability issues calls for ground-breaking solutions. In this regard, AI with its immense capabilities can offer a unique approach. This chapter aims to explore AI trends and tendencies in teaching and research and to shed light on the role of AI in sustainability education. The main research question is: How can AI be incorporated into teaching to enhance sustainability education? To achieve research aims, the qualitative research method was used and expert interview approach was applied. This research contributes to the discussion of introducing AI in sustainability education and research agenda by delving into the multifaceted intersection of AI, sustainability and education. Based on the results, a theoretical framework is proposed to adopt AI into sustainable development teaching. The findings benefit academics, educators, researchers, policymakers and industry representatives to grasp future trends in sustainability education through AI-powered initiatives.

This review examines the various ways artificial intelligence (AI) can influence school management and its potential to promote sustainable education. It brings together the findings from earlier studies to illustrate how schools are using AI to simplify administrative tasks, enrich learning experiences, and support sustainable education efforts. Key uses include AI tools for real-time data analysis, better resource management, and personalised learning paths that connect students with real-world environmental issues. By managing tasks such as data cleaning and report generation, AI enables educators and staff to dedicate more time to strategic initiatives like developing curricula and engaging the community in sustainability projects. The review also highlights major challenges and risks of using AI in education, such as concerns about data privacy, the need for reliable infrastructure, and ethical issues related to algorithmic bias. The findings show that although AI provides powerful tools for creating efficient and environmentally conscious schools, successful and fair implementation requires careful planning, targeted teacher training, and a focus on equal access. The article concludes by emphasising key areas for future research, underlining the need for robust frameworks to enable schools to use AI responsibly while promoting both academic excellence and a culture of sustainability and sustainable education.
