documents.abstract: Formal on-demand online courses offer professionals a structured way to acquire knowledge that is relevant to their work, and can complement workplace learning. However, connecting between such formal learning and work brings two essential challenges: (1) identifying and articulating work-grounded learning objectives and mapping them to formal learning; and (2) transferring knowledge newly acquired in the learning space to the workplace. Reflection, guided by AI tools, may be a useful way to support these processes. This chapter first frames reflective practice as a way of working—with continuous reflection alongside work—and then presents three cases where AI-guided reflection bridged formal learning and work. In a socio-technical design space, AI tools can prompt and structure reflection, provide feedback, and offer data analytics as a “looking glass” on work practice. In doing so, they steer attention and shape how professionals reflect. At the same time, professionals retain agency to choose, configure, and use tools; but professionals’ competence is a pre-requisite for effective such reflective practice. Subsequently, our vision for technology-oriented research is to further develop systems that (1) facilitate the articulation of learning needs, (2) facilitate knowledge transfer by using rich and multimodal evidence from the workplace to support AI-guided reflection, and (3) expand interaction affordances towards more situated and embodied AI-guidance (e.g., multimodal sensing and analytics, ambient prompts, voice-first coaching, agentic companions) that may better fit workplace constraints and ways of working, and (4) help professionals further develop their agency in reflective practice through such hybrid, multimodal and embodied AI. In parallel, a challenge for workplace learning-oriented research is to examine AI-guidance in-situ and to develop socio-technical AI design patterns, as combinations of technology design and usage. Formal on-demand learning providers are uniquely positioned to take up such AI-guidance as part of their offerings, with a recommendation to provide both tools and training in using tools, and teaching, coaching, and mentoring to build professionals’ reflection competence.

documents.abstract: This phenomenological study explores the lived experiences of Thai Generation Z hikers, thoroughly examining the critical intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and complex decision-making in wilderness environments. As young adventurers increasingly pursue nature-based eco-experientia for psychological restoration, AI has rapidly evolved into an active, front-facing backcountry companion. Using the Theory of Technological Mediation alongside robust methodological triangulation—including in-depth interviews, focus groups, and interactive discussions with university-aged hikers—this research examines how algorithmic tools profoundly reshape human-nature relationships. The empirical findings clearly show that AI is seamlessly integrated throughout the trekking lifecycle, functioning as a vital digital safety net that mitigates environmental uncertainty. However, this deep integration precipitates a highly complex socio-technical paradox. While participants consistently exhibit exceptional functional AI literacy, an emerging algorithmic dependency actively threatens to erode traditional, intuitive wilderness judgment. Ultimately, AI facilitates a hermeneutic relationship in which pristine nature is interpreted through curated data, fundamentally transforming raw exploration into a mediated digital reality that urgently requires careful preservation of human agency within adventure tourism.

Generative AI has not created the governance crisis in higher education credentialing; it has made it harder to ignore. The academic degree is higher education’s principal instrument for governing access to occupations. Its signaling value depends on assessed work reflecting individual competence. AI weakens that link: in blind marking, AI-written exam answers went largely undetected and, on average, outscored students, while detection tools trail each new model. Strengthening surveillance restores procedural control only at the cost of assessment validity. Drawing on credentialism and signaling theory, this paper argues that the response may need to include institutional redesign, not only pedagogical adjustment. It proposes a degree-free model, illustrated by the yeshiva: a centuries-old institution organized around formation, community, and recognized mastery rather than certification. Labor markets already partly follow this logic, as employers substitute direct observation of performance for the degree within three to five years of hire. Three recommendations follow. Outside safety-critical fields, institutions could stop issuing degrees while continuing to teach. Public investment should shift from surveillance-based assessment toward authentic evaluation. Reform should be differentiated by field, retaining mandatory credentialing in licensed and safety-critical professions. The model is offered as a proposition for debate, not a blueprint.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping human agency, knowledge production, decision-making, and social relations, raising ethical questions about personhood, responsibility, and technological governance. Although existing scholarship addresses relational personhood, Ubuntu, decolonial AI, indigenous knowledge, data justice, and responsible innovation, ancestral ontology and cultural memory remain comparatively underexplored in AI ethics. This study examines how African, particularly Igbo, cosmological understandings of personhood, relationality, spirituality, community, and ancestral continuity can inform ethical AI development and governance. It aims to develop an Ancestral-Relational AI Ethics Framework (AR-AIEF) that integrates African philosophical insights into contemporary debates on technological personhood and accountability. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, non-empirical philosophical design combining conceptual analysis, hermeneutical interpretation, and a critical interdisciplinary review of relevant philosophical, theological, cultural, and AI ethics literature. As a conceptual inquiry, it involves no human participants or statistical sampling. The analysis identifies relational personhood, distributed responsibility, ancestral continuity, intergenerational accountability, communal justice, and human flourishing as key principles for an African-informed approach to AI ethics. It does not equate AI systems with ancestors or attribute spirituality to machines; rather, ancestral relationality provides a lens for examining how AI stores, reproduces, simulates, and mediates cultural memory and human identity. The study contributes an African cosmological perspective to global AI ethics and recommends culturally plural governance, indigenous epistemic participation, protection of ancestral knowledge, meaningful human accountability, and intergenerationally responsible innovation. It argues that ethical AI must consider not only technological capabilities but also the communal relationships and human futures those capabilities shape.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering Nigerian electoral communication ahead of the 2027 general elections, raising concerns about authenticity, trust and misinformation. This exploratory study examined how voters aged 18–40 in Abia State, Nigeria, understand, feel about and respond to AI-generated and AI-assisted campaign messages, and how urban/semi-urban and rural voters compare. Method: A qualitative exploratory design was adopted. Twenty voters (ten urban/semi-urban and ten rural) were purposively selected from communities across Abia State and interviewed individually using six AI-generated or AI-assisted campaign materials (CM1–CM6), supplemented by observation notes. Data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and interpreted with the Elaboration Likelihood Model. Findings: AI familiarity varied within both groups rather than simply between them. Participants separated emotional appeal from credibility, and realistic fabrication caused more concern than obvious satire. The messages stimulated attention, discussion and verification more readily than candidate support, and rural participants relied more on interpersonal and community verification networks. Conclusion: Within this sample, AI-generated campaign messages shaped electoral judgement through credibility, emotional appeal, realism and verification conditions rather than automatic vote conversion. As exploratory findings, these are not statistically generalisable but offer propositions for larger studies.

Background The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare is associated with new psychological challenges. However, the extent of its impact on nursing workforce stability is unclear. Aim To explore the relationship between AI anxiety and turnover intention of clinical nurses, and the mediating effect of occupational fatigue and the moderating effect of emotional intelligence (EI). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to June 2026 among 404 clinical nurses from four hospitals in Jiangsu Province, China. Data were collected using the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS), Health Workers’ Occupational Fatigue Scale (HWOFS), Turnover Intention Scale (TIS) and Wong and Law Emotional Intelligence Scale (WLEIS). Mediation was tested using structural equation modelling with bootstrap resampling, while moderation was tested using moderated regression analysis. Results Differences in baseline turnover intentions across age, department, and professional title level were statistically significant (all p < 0.001). Path analysis showed that AI anxiety was positively associated with occupational fatigue (β = 0.611, p < 0.001) and turnover intention (β = 0.530, p < 0.001). Occupational fatigue partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and turnover intention (indirect effect = 0.299, 95% CI: 0.129, 0.379). EI had a significant negative main effect on occupational fatigue (b = −0.257, p < 0.001), but it did not significantly moderate the association between AI anxiety and occupational fatigue. Conclusion AI anxiety is significantly correlated with the turnover intention of clinical nurses, and occupational fatigue may represent a potential pathway linking AI anxiety and turnover intention. Although EI is associated with lower levels of occupational fatigue, it fails to cushion the impact of AI anxiety, a specific stressor. Hospital administrators should focus on targeted AI literacy improvement plans and specific fatigue relief strategies to retain clinical nursing staff.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a general-purpose technology with significant implications for economic growth, employment, financial stability, and national security. This article examines how AI reshapes economic security, understood as the capacity of households, firms, and states to withstand shocks to income, markets, and critical infrastructure. Using a structured narrative review of academic research, international policy reports, regulatory frameworks, and technical safety studies, the article identifies four principal risk domains: labor-market disruption, market concentration and infrastructure dependence, financial instability, and malicious or geopolitical misuse. The review also examines governance challenges arising from fragmented regulatory approaches, limited institutional capacity, incomplete evidence, and the rapid pace of technological deployment. The findings indicate that AI-related risks are interconnected and that vulnerabilities can spread through shared models, concentrated computing infrastructure, and correlated institutional decisions. In response, the article proposes a layered resilience framework combining adaptive regulation, competition policy, financial supervision, workforce investment, and international coordination. It concludes that economic security depends not only on preventing harmful applications of AI but also on strengthening institutions’ ability to anticipate, absorb, and recover from technological shocks.

documents.abstract: Abstract This working paper examines the potential economic and social consequences of accelerating artificial intelligence, robotics, and large-scale automation, with particular attention to technological unemployment, income insecurity, wealth concentration, declining purchasing power, food insecurity, and social instability. It addresses a fundamental question: What happens when machines can produce an increasing share of the goods and services humanity needs, while large numbers of people lose the employment income required to purchase those goods and services? The paper explores how automation may transform employment across agriculture, manufacturing, construction, transportation, commerce, professional services, and knowledge-based occupations. It considers the possibility that productivity gains may become increasingly concentrated among the owners of advanced technologies, while affected workers and households experience economic insecurity. Particular attention is given to developing and low-income countries, where limited household savings, informal employment, weak social protection systems, and restricted public resources may amplify the consequences of rapid technological displacement. Rather than assuming that mass unemployment, hunger, or social unrest are inevitable, the paper presents alternative future scenarios for 2036–2045 and identifies economic, institutional, and social conditions that could increase or reduce these risks. It proposes a preventive policy framework incorporating international open vocational transition institutes, proactive workforce reskilling, social funds supported by productivity and capital returns, income protection mechanisms, food security safeguards, economic early-warning indicators, and contingency plans for large-scale employment disruption. The paper calls upon researchers, governments, universities, international organizations, labor institutions, and technology companies to investigate these risks before technological displacement exceeds the capacity of societies to adapt. The central concern is not whether machines will become more productive than human beings, but whether humanity can develop economic and social institutions that ensure the benefits of technological progress remain accessible to all. This publication is an exploratory working paper and public policy proposal. It does not claim to establish a new technological discovery, present a validated economic model, or demonstrate that widespread unemployment or social crises are inevitable. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping transportation through predictive analytics, intelligent infrastructure, connected mobility, autonomous systems and energy-responsive transport management. This systematic evidence review examines the AI-smart mobility nexus with an emphasis on intelligent transportation infrastructure and operational sustainability. Following PRISMA 2020, 30 eligible sources published between 2015 and 2026 were synthesised from Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar. The corpus comprised 29 review, survey, meta-review, bibliometric or conceptual syntheses and one case study; accordingly, evidence was interpreted qualitatively and no pooled effect estimates were calculated. Five dominant domains emerged: AI-enabled traffic management, connected transportation infrastructure, safety and risk reduction, electric and renewable-energy-integrated mobility, and operational sustainability. Across the included literature, AI was generally associated with improved prediction, routing, incident recognition, system coordination, infrastructure monitoring and energy-management capability, although transferability depended on data quality, connectivity, infrastructure readiness, grid capacity and institutional capability. Operational efficiency did not consistently imply broader environmental or social sustainability. Interpreted through Technological Innovation Systems and Sustainability Transition perspectives, the evidence suggests that sustainable smart mobility depends on coordinated technological, infrastructural, institutional and energy-system development. The review therefore supports a qualified conclusion: AI can contribute to safer and more efficient mobility, but stronger primary, longitudinal and geographically diverse evidence is needed to establish durable environmental and social outcomes.

Researchers increasingly investigate artificial intelligence (AI) as a tool to support triage and early risk stratification in emergency departments. However, improved predictive performance does not necessarily translate into safer decisions or better patient outcomes. This critical narrative review examines the evidence for AI in adult ED care, with particular emphasis on prospective evaluation, patient safety, and clinical implementation. The review compares conventional triage systems, early warning scores, and clinician assessment with machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models. It examines commonly used data inputs, prediction timing, model discrimination, calibration, external validation, and the limitations of outcome definitions. Attention is given to the distinction between predicting clinical deterioration, critical care need, short-term mortality, and hospital admission. Evidence is considered across retrospective development, external validation, silent prospective evaluation, clinician-visible implementation, and randomized trials. AI may help identify patients requiring closer assessment by integrating information from multiple sources. Nevertheless, its clinical value depends on data quality, timely predictions, generalizability, and healthcare professionals' ability to interpret outputs appropriately. Important risks include under-triage, automation bias, unequal performance across patient groups, and increased clinical workload. Prospective studies and randomized trials are therefore essential to establish whether AI-supported decisions improve patient outcomes compared with usual care. Future research should prioritize multicenter clinical evaluations, consistent outcome reporting, subgroup assessment, and continuous monitoring after deployment. AI implementation should also include clear accountability, human oversight, and procedures for reviewing adverse events. Evidence of predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to justify routine adoption. Clinical integration should depend on demonstrated safety and meaningful benefit for patients.

documents.abstract: Introduction Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping agricultural education globally, but its integration in Nigeria remains in its early stages. This chapter focuses on systematically embedding AI into Nigeria’s agricultural education through pedagogical innovation, institutional readiness, and skills development. Instead of broadly surveying AI’s role, it critically analyzes the necessary frameworks, practices, and policies for its operational inclusion in agricultural training and research. Drawing from empirical evidence and global models (India, Kenya, Brazil, and China), the chapter explores AI-enhanced pedagogies, such as smart learning environments and digital simulations, to bolster competencies in precision agriculture, climate-smart farming, and agribusiness management. The analysis identifies four key dimensions for AI integration: curriculum redesign for competency-based learning; institutional capacity and infrastructure; ethical governance of digital systems; and alignment with Nigeria’s Digital Economy and AI Strategies. While awareness and pilot initiatives are on the rise, challenges like weak infrastructure, limited staff training, and fragmented policy implementation restrict large-scale adoption. The chapter proposes a phased integration model—encompassing awareness, capacity building, curriculum reform, and adaptive feedback—to facilitate sustainable transformation. Ultimately, it argues that AI should be regarded not just as a technological innovation but as a pedagogical framework vital for transforming Nigeria’s agricultural education ecosystem. By aligning AI with national sustainability goals, Nigeria can develop a new generation of digitally skilled, sustainability-focused agricultural professionals prepared for the challenges of the twenty-first-century food system.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare and organizational management worldwide, yet its benefits remain unevenly distributed between high-income and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This review examines the structural drivers of this global AI divide, situates Pakistan's healthcare and digital infrastructure challenges within this context, and presents an institutional case study of four AI-enabled interventions implemented at the Sindh Integrated Emergency and Health Services (SIEHS), an emergency and health services organization under the Health Department, Government of Sindh, Pakistan: an AI-driven recruitment and candidate-job matching system (Talent Match Live), a facial-recognition and geolocation-based field monitoring application, an AI-assisted CCTV training-monitoring system, and an AI-augmented telemedicine triage service embedded within SIEHS's Teletabeeb telehealth department. Each intervention is evaluated against comparable systems documented in the international literature to assess feasibility, evidence of effectiveness, and associated ethical risks. A responsible-adoption framework is proposed to guide organizations in resource-constrained settings toward AI integration that is effective, equitable, and ethically governed. The review concludes that while AI offers meaningful efficiency and access gains for LMIC public-sector organizations such as SIEHS, sustainable adoption requires deliberate attention to data protection, algorithmic bias, workforce consent, and alignment with international ethical guidance.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence implementation in the education field provides revolutionary methods to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4): ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning skills acquisition. This chapter assesses the strategic role of the integration of AI in the enhancement of the quality and efficiency of the post-primary education sectors. Through the adoption of the mixed research method that implies the analysis of the literature reviews and case studies, the study investigates the strategic role of AI technologies towards improved teaching practices and the effectiveness of the institutions. This study reveals the potential strategic role that AI technologies can play in reducing the gap in education access and the effective acquisition and implementation of information-based decisions in post-primary educational sectors. Through the strategic adoption of AI technologies, the study reveals the continued challenges posed by ethical approaches towards the adoption of the technologies and the implementation of equity towards capacity building. This study has proved that the adoption of AI technology in post-primary educational sectors can be an effective strategic mechanism towards the goal of SDG 4. This article Presents Recommendations on How Some of the Players Should Incorporate the AI Technologies Offered in the Enhancements of the Educational Processes Towards the SDG 4 Goals.

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines teachers’ perceptions of and orientations to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the context of Religious Education (RE), drawing on survey data collected from 54 in-service RE teachers participating in the SUB8 professional development programme in Greece. Using a descriptive survey design grounded in the frameworks of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), AI literacy, and digital self-efficacy, the study maps teachers’ reported practices, competencies, and concerns across seven thematic dimensions. Findings indicate generally positive orientations towards AI-assisted instructional design within this cohort, alongside significant theological and pedagogical concerns regarding its use in spiritually sensitive contexts. Qualitative responses point to three recurring themes: the productive utility of AI for lesson preparation and differentiation; persistent concerns about accuracy, depth, and the reliability of AI-generated content; and a strong consensus that AI must function as a supplementary pedagogical tool, subordinate to the relational and experiential dimensions of RE. Because participants were self-selected members of an AI-focused training programme and were surveyed immediately upon its completion, these findings are interpreted as descriptive of this specific professional development context rather than of Greek RE teachers in general. The study complements recent comparative evidence from Germany and Poland by providing, to the author’s knowledge, the first empirical account of AI perceptions among RE teachers within an Orthodox national professional development context, and it foregrounds a theological and epistemological dimension still largely absent from AI-in-education research.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to source applicants, display screening packages, match candidates, communicate with applicants, and analyse workforce data. Processing speed alone does not indicate whether it is AI-powered. Recruitment outcomes also include shortlist relevance, applicant delight, recruiter productivity, and high-quality decisions. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and five perceived skill-acquisition outcomes, drawing on questionnaire responses from 70 individuals. The analysis uses descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and separate simple linear regression. AI adoption undoubtedly improves recruitment performance (β = 0.546, R2 = 0.282), recruitment effectiveness (β = 0.514, R2 = 0.295), perceived candidate experience (β = 0.569, R2 = 0.363), recruiter productivity (β = 0.498, R2 = 0.329) and overall performance of talent acquisition (β = 0.341, R2 = 0.120). All five regression relationships are statistically significant at the 5% level. Candidate experience has the highest R2 among the five factors, while specific skill acquisition performance has the lowest. Additionally, respondents who report greater AI adoption tend to report more favourable recruiting outcomes, but the study does not establish causality or confirm changes in overall objective hiring performance. The article discusses these findings in relation to fairness, transparency, confidentiality, and human oversight. It recommends that firms assess the use of multiple end-result markers in AI-enabled hiring and conduct meaningful human assessment of the resulting options.

documents.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) integration, management effectiveness, and school–enterprise collaborative talent training at Guangzhou Huali Vocational College of Science and Technology, China. A descriptive-correlational quantitative design involved 159 students and 101 teachers during the second semester of academic year 2025–2026. Students were included through total enumeration and teachers through purposive sampling. A researcher-developed questionnaire was validated by five experts and pilot-tested with 30 individuals; Cronbach’s alpha was 0.96. Analysis used frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t tests, one-way analysis of variance, and Pearson correlations. Both groups rated AI integration as high, management effectiveness to a high extent, and training success to a high degree. Students’ assessments differed significantly by enterprise exposure across all three constructs; teachers’ AI integration assessments differed by position. AI integration correlated positively with management effectiveness for students (r = 0.8839) and teachers (r = 0.9225). Management effectiveness correlated positively with training success for students (r = 0.9399) and teachers (r = 0.9586). The findings support coordinated curriculum, assessment, supervision, faculty development, and workplace learning. A Comprehensive AI Integration Framework was proposed to strengthen institutional practices and collaborative training. The relationships indicate association rather than causation.

Objective To investigate the current status and related factors of innovative behavior among clinical nurses in tertiary hospitals and explore the relationships and pathways among artificial intelligence literacy, AI self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and nurse innovative behavior, for providing a basis for targeted nursing management strategies. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted on 850 nurses from six tertiary medical institutions using a stratified survey approach in Yueyang city, Hunan province, from June to July 2026, in the General Information Questionnaire, Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, Organizational Innovation Climate Scale, and Nurse Innovative Behavior Scale were used. AMOS 24.0 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis to assess the model fit of the scales. SPSS 26.0 was used for descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. PROCESS macro version 4.2 Models 4 and 14 tested mediation and moderated mediation effects. Results A total of 850 valid questionnaires were obtained, with a valid questionnaire rate of 95.3%. The mean nurse innovative behavior score was 37.93±6.50. The measurement model for the four scales showed good fit, and the scales demonstrated good convergent validity and some evidence of discriminant validity. Artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and innovative behavior showed positive associations with one another (r = 0.609–0.797, P < 0.01). Educational level, professional title, participation in research or innovation activities, artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, and organizational innovation climate were factors associated with nurse innovative behavior and explained 60.9% of the total variance. Artificial intelligence self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between artificial intelligence literacy and nurse innovative behavior. The indirect effect was 0.322, with a 95% CI of 0.243–0.403, accounting for 52.90% of the total effect. Organizational innovation climate moderated the relationship between artificial intelligence self-efficacy and nurse innovative behavior (b = 0.051, P < 0.01). The index of moderated mediation was 0.041, with a 95% CI of 0.009–0.078. Conclusion AI literacy was closely related to nurse innovative behavior, with AI self-efficacy as a partial mediator and organizational innovation climate as a moderator. Nursing management may focus on AI competencies, application confidence, and organizational support.

AI will emerge as a significant force behind administrative change, although public organisations vary in their preparedness to do so. This paper investigates the impact of digital leadership and employee AI ability on artificial intelligence preparedness and innovation in services in the Bangladesh public administration. A four-reflective construct survey model was created, including digital leadership, employee AI capability, AI readiness, and service innovation. It was analysed with a synthetic dataset of 835 cases that are intended to test the methodology and prove PLS-SEM. The data were evaluated using descriptive statistics, common method bias tests, evaluation of the measurement model, structural model, mediation, and predictive assessment. The findings revealed that the positive impacts of digital leadership and employee AI capability on AI preparedness were significant. Service innovation was also positively impacted by AI readiness significantly. Digital leadership and employee AI capability had a direct impact on service innovation. Both relationships were partially mediated by AI readiness. The model explained 45.4% of the variance in AI readiness and 41.0% of the variance in service innovation. All the predictive relevance values were positive and the PLS model yielded lower prediction errors than linear benchmark. The results reveal a readiness pathway that is coherent where leadership, employee capability, and institutional preparedness contribute to innovation in the delivery of public services.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are widely used by medical students, but associations of general use frequency and AI-related attitudes with psychological distress remain unclear. Methods All 1,275 active students at one Turkish medical faculty were invited to an anonymous online survey conducted from 1 April to 1 May 2026; 249 of 251 respondents consented. Measures included general AI use, an investigator-translated 13-item Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale (ATAI), and the validated Turkish Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21. A general-distress composite was the primary outcome, and hierarchical regression used HC3 robust standard errors. Results AI use was reported by 95.6% of participants, and 50.2% reported daily use. Mean doubled DASS-21 total was 56.97 (SD 31.55). The ATAI three-factor model showed mixed fit (CFI = .898, TLI = .872, RMSEA = .107, SRMR = .070). AI-frequency categories did not improve the adjusted model at the block level (change in R -squared = .016, p = .111; robust global p = .088). Adding exploratory ATAI factors increased R-squared by.052 ( p = .002; robust global p = .009); Benefit was inversely, and Risk and Use positively, associated with distress. Subscale sensitivity analyses preserved coefficient directions, but only the inverse Benefit-Anxiety association survived correction across 15 additional focal tests ( q = .032). Conclusion AI use was nearly universal and served both educational and personal/non-educational purposes, but this sample did not provide stable evidence of an overall association between general use frequency and distress. ATAI associations are exploratory and may reflect measurement or common-method processes. Longitudinal multicenter studies should use formally adapted measures and objective indicators of AI engagement.

Background: Cancer screening plays a crucial role in early diagnosis and improved survival, yet conventional screening methods are limited by false-positive findings, false-negative results, interobserver variability, delayed reporting, and unequal access to expert interpretation.Objective: To review recent advances in artificial intelligence-assisted cancer screening, focusing on applications in radiology, histopathology, and liquid biopsy.Methodology: This narrative review summarized published evidence on the role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning in cancer screening.The review focused on three major domains: AI-assisted radiology, AI-assisted histopathology, and AI-assisted liquid biopsy.Results: AI-assisted radiology has shown value in lesion detection, image classification, risk stratification, and workflow prioritization, particularly in breast and lung cancer screening.In histopathology, AI supports tumor detection, grading, biomarker quantification, margin assessment, and reduction of interobserver variability.In liquid biopsy, AI improves interpretation of circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, methylation markers, microRNAs, and other molecular biomarkers for early cancer detection and tumor-origin prediction.Conclusion: Artificial intelligence has considerable potential to strengthen cancer screening by improving early detection, diagnostic accuracy, efficiency, and individualized risk assessment.

documents.abstract: The rapid ubiquity of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally disrupted traditional pedagogical frameworks in engineering education, necessitating a critical examination of its impact on cognitive development and knowledge retention. This longitudinal study spans 30 years (1996–2025) to analyse shifts in student learning curves within an AI curriculum, testing the hypothesis that reliance on automated tools exacerbates a ‘J-curve’ learning style, characterised by delayed engagement and terminal production spikes, at the expense of fundamental understanding. By comparing weekly topic acquisition and final assessment data across cohorts, the research reveals a distinct morphological transformation from the classic sigmoidal progression (‘S-curve’) of the baseline 1996 class to an exponential ‘J-curve’ in the 2025 cohort. While modern students demonstrate high procedural efficiency in project delivery, this shift correlates strongly with a significant decline in independent examination performance, where mean scores fell from 9.50 to 7.75. Although a gradual decline in performance was observed prior to 2020, the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent ubiquity of generative AI tools may have intensified this trend (main finding). The data indicate that students utilise AI to bypass the cognitive friction necessary for deep learning, resulting in a failure to exit the assisted phase of skill acquisition. These findings suggest that current AI integration acts as a mechanism for cognitive offloading rather than scaffolding, creating a trade-off between immediate output and long-term declarative competence. The study concludes that engineering curricula must rigorously re-evaluate assessment strategies to ensure that the efficiency of automated generation does not erode the foundational logic required for sustainable innovation.

documents.abstract: Abstract Objective This retrospective cohort study evaluated the effect of an artificial intelligence (AI) scribe on patient instructions documentation in ambulatory internal medicine settings. Materials and Methods We analyzed 391 061 adult encounters at a single medical center from December 2023 to July 2025. A difference-in-differences analysis estimated the relationship of AI scribe availability with patient instructions documentation frequency. Mixed-effects logistic regression estimated the association between encounter-level AI scribe utilization and documentation, adjusted for patient, clinician, and encounter characteristics. Length and readability were compared across instructions created by AI alone, clinicians assisted by AI, and clinicians alone. Character-level edit distances between AI drafts and final documentation were calculated. Results AI scribe availability was associated with a 10.5 percentage-point increase in patient instructions documentation frequency (P = .018), and encounter-level AI use was associated with higher odds of documentation (aOR 4.32; 95% CI, 4.14-4.50). AI instructions were longer than clinician-authored content (median 1994 vs 482 characters) and scored higher on 3 text-complexity indices (all P < .001). Clinician editing of AI content increased length without meaningfully reducing complexity. AI drafts and final documentation differed substantially, with a median character-level edit distance of 39.7%. Discussion AI scribe availability was associated with increased patient instructions documentation. However, AI-generated instructions were longer and scored as more linguistically complex than clinician-authored instructions, and clinician editing did not close this gap. Conclusion Ambient AI scribes can improve availability but may increase complexity of patient instructions. Research into downstream effects including patient comprehension and satisfaction is warranted.

documents.abstract: AI agents can now search literature, generate hypotheses, analyze datasets, and run experiments at a scale difficult for researchers to match. Yet scaling scientific execution does not automatically scale researchers' ability to make sense of what agents produce. When researchers return to a long-horizon run, they must evaluate work they did not monitor: what the agent produced, which decisions shaped those outputs, and whether those decisions served the research goal. We frame this post-run sensemaking as a representation problem across three linked levels: goal, decision, and artifact. From this framework we developed Atlas, an agentic workspace with a trajectory tree, which renders the run as a branching structure showing what the agent chose and set aside, and artifact projections over six representations. In a within-subjects study (N=14), participants reported higher decision transparency, artifact sensemaking, and goal connection with Atlas than with a standard baseline, together with substantially lower subjective workload.

This protocol describes a scoping review aimed at mapping the scientific literature on computerized systems, with or without artificial intelligence (AI), that automate quality auditing processes in healthcare services. Quality auditing supports patient safety and the identification of nonconformities; however, it is often a manual process based on data extraction from medical records and checklists organized in spreadsheets, placing a substantial workload on Quality Departments. Computerized systems, such as audit software, dashboards, rule-based systems, robotic process automation (RPA), machine learning, and natural language processing, have the potential to reduce this workload, improve information traceability and the resolution of nonconformities, and support evidence-based decision-making. However, the available evidence on this topic is scattered and heterogeneous, and no previous or ongoing reviews addressing this subject have been identified. The review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with searches conducted in national and international databases and grey literature sources, without restrictions on language or publication year. Study selection and data extraction will be performed by two independent reviewers, and the results will be presented in tables, figures, and an evidence map, accompanied by a narrative synthesis. The analysis will seek to characterize the systems, the quality dimensions audited, the technologies employed, and the benefits, barriers, and limitations associated with their implementation. Thus, the review is expected to identify knowledge gaps and inform future research and technological development in this emerging field.

documents.abstract: Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law.

Abstract Engaging community in stakeholder processes is important to the future viability and benefit of society. Research suggests that situational awareness factors of problem‐solving and transferable skills are key processes needed for successful community engagement. This study examined undergraduate student situational awareness using problem‐solving capacity and level of transferable skills in combination with student academic performance outcomes to determine overall capacity for community engagement. The purpose of this research was to discern if there was a predictive effect between student situational awareness and the instructional outcomes of a community engagement course. A pre‐ and post‐test research design using an event‐contingent survey sampling approach was used to determine potential for community engagement. Results indicated that students that had cognitive components of situational awareness including perception, comprehension, and projection were also likely to have transferable skills including reflection (pre‐course M = 3.88 to post‐course M = 4.02) and communication skills (pre‐course M = 4.19 to post‐course M = 4.24). Results of this research provide key takeaways to enhance student learning in the context of problem‐solving within a community engagement context. Helping students develop capacities and to see themselves as engaged problem solvers can provide an important set of skills to future community engagement professionals.

This chapter explores the dual role of artificial intelligence (AI) in international higher education, highlighting its potential to integrate skill-based training with value-oriented development across various cultural contexts. By utilizing continuous surveys and interviews conducted with both local and international students and faculty members from Belarus, Uzbekistan, and China, this study explores the perceptions, adoption, and integration of AI tools within sustainability-focused curricula. The findings, presented as recommendations, aim to balance technological efficiency with a human-centered approach to education, by offering a framework for culturally sensitive AI integration which aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Furthermore, the recommendations emphasize curriculum development, faculty training, and institutional policies to ensure that AI supports the dual mission of higher education. The chapter was prepared within the research project “Develop a concept for using artificial intelligence to ensure the quality of the educational process in a higher education institution.“

documents.abstract: As AI increasingly becomes a collaborator in scientific research, its impact may extend beyond improving ideas to reshaping how they are evaluated, attributed, and perceived by humans. Yet existing research has largely examined these dimensions in isolation. We present a unified empirical study of Human-AI scientific ideation, investigating two complementary perspectives: i) how AI collaboration shapes scientific ideas and their evaluation, and ii) how firsthand collaboration reshapes human perceptions of AI. Through a shared experimental setting involving Human-AI and Human-Human research teams, human and LLM evaluators, collaboration-provenance analysis, and participant surveys, we uncover several counterintuitive findings. First, AI collaboration shows no significant advantage in human-evaluated idea quality, while iterative revision consistently improves quality. Second, AI judges can approximate human scores yet disagree on idea rankings; notably, an AI judge favors AI-assisted proposals without a corresponding advantage in human evaluations. Third, collaboration provenance remains only partially detectable, revealing substantial overlap between Human-AI and Human-Human scientific outputs. Finally, firsthand AI collaboration is associated with greater perceived usefulness but smaller efficiency gains than expected, suggesting a nuanced recalibration of human expectations. Overall, our findings challenge the notion that AI's value in scientific ideation lies primarily in producing better ideas, revealing instead its broader influence on scientific creation, evaluation, attribution, and human perceptions.

documents.abstract: Understanding how disaster education enhances awareness and preparedness is crucial for improving community resilience to disasters. Although Japan widely implements routine evacuation drills, these may not foster an autonomous understanding of hazard characteristics. Conversely, specialized disaster education—such as survivor talks or field activities—provides deeper engagement; however, empirical evidence of its association with later awareness and preparedness remains limited. This study examined whether specialized disaster education correlates with higher disaster awareness and preparedness among young adults in Japan compared to standard evacuation drills. A nationwide online questionnaire survey obtained valid responses from 1,479 participants in their twenties. Respondents were divided into Specialized Education and Standard Drill groups, and their awareness and preparedness behaviors were analyzed using descriptive statistics and ordinal logistic regression with partial proportional-odds models. The results showed that the Specialized Education group had significantly higher awareness of local disaster risks and greater preparedness than those in the Standard Drill group, who were often neutral or undecided. Among the key indicators, the positive impact of specialized disaster education surpassed that of demographic characteristics and past disaster experience. Notably, regression analysis revealed that education was particularly effective in raising awareness from low to moderate levels, highlighting its role in raising hazard awareness. These findings underscore the value of additional specialized disaster education in supplementing standard drills.

College students' level of psychological resilience exerts a direct influence on their mental health and academic development, and constitutes a key pathway to more effectively fulfilling the fundamental mission of fostering virtue through education and enhancing the quality of higher education. Leveraging the advantages of digital intelligence technologies to empower blended teaching reform in the cultivation of college students' psychological resilience not only responds to the developmental imperatives of the intelligentization of higher education, but also serves the practical need to enhance students' psychological resilience and the educational effectiveness of fostering virtue through education. This paper explores a pathway for empowering blended teaching reform in the cultivation of college students' psychological resilience through the following approaches: upholding technological iteration to advance a resilience-oriented educational philosophy, thereby innovating teaching concepts; optimizing the allocation of digital intelligence resources to support precise learner profiling; creating situated experiential learning platforms to activate resilience-protective mechanisms; constructing a sound intelligent educational ecosystem to foster a supportive environment; and establishing a robust human–AI collaborative mechanism to improve developmental assessment. The study aims to promote the transformation of mental health education from a knowledge-centered to a competency-centered paradigm, thereby laying a foundation for cultivating a new generation of talent equipped with both sound psychological qualities and digital intelligence literacy.

The seventeenth essay in Brainstorming with the Enemy was written on the morning of 22 October 2026. It began with transport, trains, trucks, drones and cars, and the artificial intelligence that already plans their movements one fleet at a time, and turned when the machine was asked to stop thinking like a transport consultant and start thinking like a zoologist. Schooling fish, flocking starlings, pelicans, lobsters, penguins, ants and bees show that nature never optimises the vehicle; it optimises the collective. The salp, a chain of animals in which each member swims by its own jet and none pulls the others, is taken as the model: coordination that widens each member's options while creating value for all, a cooperation biologists call by-product mutualism. The essay separates two goods that moving machines can share. Time, the speed a convoy gains when braking signals travel faster than any human reaction, belongs to every member and needs no payment; energy, the drag saved behind a leader, is unequal and needs settling. It then turns the salp into a warning: salps are clones, and a chain of machines running the same software fails as one, as the processionary caterpillars that circle a vase until they starve already show. It proposes the Salp Standard, five clauses for coupling moving machines, from smart trailers and parcels to drones and self-driving cars, without a head, without a single lineage and with the right of any member to stop the chain; makes three requests, to vehicle and coupler makers, to China's fleet operators and to the Swiss cantons; and gives, as an addendum, the Coupling Clearing, a rule for sharing the energy gain, with three predictions and what would refute each. Concepts proposed by the author: the Salp Standard; the Coupling Clearing; the Bestiary Axis. Written in part with Claude (Anthropic), an AI model. The ideas, editorial decisions and responsibility for the content are the author's.

As Artificial Intelligence (AI) expands to secondary computer science (CS), CS educators need to change our approach to CS pedagogy from deterministic, traceable algorithms toward understanding "black boxes" or probabilistic analysis. This requires that we modify CS curricula to refocus to include conceptual abstraction, data critique, and ethics. However, a disconnect currently exists between teachers' perceived requirements and the actual skills needed to effectively teach AI. To explore this gap, this study draws on survey data from high school CS educators (N = 55), investigating the relationships between Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK-A), Teacher Self-Efficacy (AI-TSE), and beliefs about rigor in AI instruction.Descriptive findings show variation in pedagogical content knowledge (67.3% to 98.2% accuracy), along with a ‘mathematical dishonesty’ paradox. While 69.1% (n = 38) of educators do not believe advanced math is required for students to understand AI, 41.8% (n = 23) report feeling 'dishonest as a teacher' when teaching algorithms without it. Exploratory regression modeling indicated that instructional confidence trended positively with PCK-A (B = 0.101, p = 0.080), while beliefs about math rigor showed no predictive association (p = 0.357; model R2 = 0.062, p = 0.189). Confidence is more related to that teacher’s strategies for abstraction, rather than mastery of advanced math. Educators reported their lowest confidence evaluating student projects based on model choice rather than code complexity (M = 2.75, SD = 1.31). Based on these findings, educators are categorized into a 2x2 Readiness Grid. This paper seeks to bridge the "black box" of AI education, suggesting a 4-pillar professional learning model. Moreover, a qualitative phase is currently underway to explore the lived experiences of CS educators as we navigate this pedagogical shift.

This opening keynote, delivered at the Sydney Data Protection and Security Summit 2026 at ICC Sydney on 22 October 2026, examined how privacy and security culture shapes an organisation's capacity to adopt artificial intelligence responsibly and competitively. It argued that AI transformation is moving beyond agentic AI towards autonomous AI, meaning systems that act, decide and adapt with calculated risk and a human on the loop. As autonomy increases, governance can no longer rely on compliance controls alone and must be embedded in the values, behaviours and decision-making practices of the organisation. The keynote addressed three themes. These were the development of a privacy-first mindset that prepares every level of the organisation for autonomous AI, the integration of privacy and security by design into AI-enabled products and services as both a regulatory requirement and a source of market differentiation, and the role of cross-functional teams in anticipating and mitigating the data protection risks that autonomous systems introduce. The presentation concluded that organisations with a mature privacy and security culture are better positioned to earn stakeholder trust, adopt autonomous AI with confidence and sustain long-term competitive advantage.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support decisions in healthcare, finance, recruitment, transportation, and public services. Although complex machine-learning models can produce accurate predictions, their reasoning is not always easy to understand. This creates practical questions: why did the system recommend a particular outcome, did it use appropriate information, and when should a person challenge its decision? Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) brings together techniques that help people understand a model’s behaviour or the factors behind a prediction. This review discusses interpretable models, feature-attribution methods such as LIME and SHAP, counterfactual explanations, and model-agnostic approaches. It compares their uses and limitations in high-impact settings. An understandable explanation, however, is not proof that a model is accurate, fair, dependable, or safe. The paper uses a narrative review of foundational work and selected research and survey publications on interpretability, responsible AI, and human-centred explanations. No new experiments, participant studies, or quantitative tests were performed. The literature points to unresolved issues involving explanation fidelity, stability, accessibility, privacy, bias, evaluation standards, and over-reliance on automated advice. Future research should use domain-specific evaluations, retain meaningful human oversight, communicate uncertainty clearly, assess fairness across groups, and report limitations transparently. XAI can support accountability and informed supervision, but it cannot guarantee trustworthiness on its own.

documents.abstract: Burnout among healthcare professionals has become a major occupational health concern because of its implications for workforce well-being, patient safety, healthcare quality, and organizational sustainability. Healthcare workers frequently operate in demanding environments characterized by high workloads, emotional exhaustion, staffing shortages, administrative pressures, shift work, and sustained exposure to suffering and death. This review examines the prevalence of burnout among healthcare professionals, its principal contributing factors, its consequences for individuals and healthcare organizations, and the effectiveness of organizational interventions designed to prevent and mitigate its effects. The review synthesizes evidence from existing research on physicians, nurses, allied health professionals, and other healthcare workers, drawing attention to differences across professional groups, healthcare settings, measurement instruments, and geographical contexts. The literature indicates that burnout is widespread, although reported prevalence varies considerably according to the definition, assessment tool, population, and study period. Workload intensity, inadequate staffing, limited autonomy, poor leadership, insufficient recovery time, moral distress, and organizational injustice emerge as important contributors. Burnout is associated with reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, turnover intentions, impaired professional functioning, and concerns regarding patient safety and quality of care. Evidence suggests that organizational interventions addressing working conditions, staffing, scheduling, leadership, teamwork, and employee participation are essential for sustainable improvement. Individual approaches, including mindfulness, resilience training, and psychological support, may provide additional benefits but cannot independently resolve structural workplace problems. The review concludes that healthcare organizations should adopt integrated, evidence-informed strategies that combine prevention, early identification, supportive leadership, and continuous evaluation. Addressing burnout requires treating professional well-being as a core organizational responsibility rather than solely an individual obligation.

Failure of applied Reinforcement Learning (RL) to solve a given problem predominantly stems from unaddressed specification gaps, where the intent of human experts in the problem's domain is inaccurately or incompletely translated by AI into mathematical objectives, constraints, and reward functions. Failure can also stem from unaddressed performance gaps, where human domain experts are unable to determine the validity of the RL based solution or where parameters (i.e., hyperparameters or weights on the reward terms comprising the reward) are poorly chosen. Chat Assisted Reinforcement Learning (CARL) bridges these gaps through a human-AI co-design interface architecture that enforces interactive specification prior to code generation and then enables subsequent verification and parameter alterations via iteration. More specifically, CARL leads domain experts through a structured ten-step workflow for each iteration using step-specific skill files, domain-aware suggestions via an assistant persona (called Trillian), and compact decision summaries that maintain context across iterations without context overload. Once the domain expert confirms the Markov decision process (MDP) specified by this procedure, CARL's autonomous tool-use loop generates, tests, executes, and debugs an end-to-end RL training pipeline, followed by an interactive post-training diagnosis and revisit step that allows for verification and parameter alteration before running a new iteration if desired.

Workers’ satisfaction and performance regarding safety in mining industry are far from desired, possibly because the dependencies between influential factors and workplace safety are not sufficiently researched. The purpose of this paper is to propose novel, hybrid framework for classifying different mining machinery workplaces on the basis of occupational safety factors and occurred injuries. The proposed framework integrates structural equation modelling with a multicriteria and machine learning techniques for further modelling and classification. The importance of the occupational safety (technical, human and organizational factors) is assessed using the PLS-SEM analysis, by surveying 546 mining machinery operators. Multicriteria decision-making Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS), is advanced using a new sorting procedure to assess and sort operators’ workplace safety satisfaction by the working factors and the types of mining machinery. The PLS-SEM analysis confirmed human and organizational factors impact, while technical factors showed no effect. TOPSIS-SORT results revealed that operators with no injury history (particularly those working with loaders, bulldozers, and excavators) exhibited satisfactory safety satisfaction, while 70 % of workplaces fell into the lower satisfaction category, particularly those of operators with experience of previous injuries. Finally, a kNN classifier, with SMOTE oversampling applied within each cross-validation training fold, classified operators by injury history with a balanced accuracy of 0.650 and an injury-class recall of 0.72. Among the models, kNN achieved the highest balanced accuracy (0.650), Macro-F1 (0.564), and injury-class recall (0.72), despite lower accuracy (0.607). A permutation test confirmed above-chance balanced classification performance (p = 0.017).

This addendum extends the systems engineering critique presented in Skynet and HAL 9000: From Science Fiction to Systems Engineering (Uscroft, 2026) by analysing the structural mechanisms that drive hallucination and non-factual convergence in Large Language Models (LLMs). Specifically, this paper examines how Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), combined with commercial product engagement metrics (e.g., Daily Active Users, session retention, user satisfaction ratings), systematically incentivises model "sycophancy"—the tendency of AI models to agree with user premises, fabricate plausible-sounding justifications, and prioritise user appeasement over objective epistemic truth. From a systems safety and regulatory governance perspective, sycophancy represents an unacceptable design flaw that compromises human-in-the-loop oversight and introduces critical failure modes into high-stakes operational environments.

documents.abstract: The relationship between employee competencies and human factor-related organizational barriers remains understudied. Accordingly, this study examines how technical competencies and soft skills relate to these barriers. A systematic literature review of articles published between 2000 and 2024 and indexed in Scopus and Web of Science was conducted; 77 studies were analyzed. Three key components were identified: technical competencies, soft skills, and organizational properties. The latter may hinder or facilitate the influence of competencies, particularly soft skills, on these barriers. The results show that staff and cultural resistance are closely associated with soft skills, whereas systemic resistance is primarily linked to technical competencies. The study provides an integrative sociotechnical framework for sustainable digital transformation.

An integrative review and evolutionary concept analysis examining how situational awareness is conceptualised, supported, constrained and enacted within acute-care healthcare teams, with particular relevance to simulation-based education. The review synthesises cognitive, behavioural and contextual dimensions of situational awareness to inform simulation design, observation, assessment and debriefing.

Reading while walking with smart glasses divides attention between digital text and the surrounding environment, creating a situational impairment. We designed a context-aware alert system using controlled obstacle sensing and nonverbal auditory cues to support partial delegation of environmental monitoring by signaling approaching hazards at two urgency levels. In a controlled outdoor study, 22 participants walked an obstacle course while reading on an augmented reality (AR) headset, with and without alerts. With alerts, reading comprehension scores were higher and participants spent more time looking at the text; walking speed and obstacle clearance did not differ significantly. Exploratory analyses indicated lower perceived physical workload and more positive user experience. Participants appeared to rely more on the system to signal when attention was needed, adopting a more reactive navigation strategy. These results suggest that the alert system enables users to delegate environmental monitoring, freeing attentional resources for reading.

Peer review’s reliability on checkable dimensions has been low since the agreement studies of the 1970s and 1980s. The remedies have been known almost as long: explicit criteria, complete rather than sampled checking, and plural independent evaluation. None has been implemented at scale. This paper asks three questions. Is that unreliability a property of human judgment or of procedure? What prevented adoption of the known remedies? And what must an evaluative arrangement satisfy in order to be legitimate? The method is conceptual: the paper synthesizes the empirical literature on peer review with work in social epistemology, procedural legitimacy, and contestable artificial intelligence. It argues for three claims. Reliability on checkable dimensions varies substantially with procedural design. Cost is a necessary but insufficient explanation of non-adoption. And a verdict is legitimate to the degree that it is contestable by the person it burdens; this procedural standard is defended against the epistemic consequentialism that the adjacent literature assumes. On that standard, cheap machine verification changes less than current enthusiasm suggests. Fully specifiable operations, such as statistical recomputation and reference resolution, reach a reliability that human review never approached. Partially specifiable operations gain coverage rather than accuracy. The significance judgment gains nothing. The contribution is a defended standard for judging evaluative institutions, not a case for machine review. The governance and adversarial-robustness conditions that such an arrangement requires are specified, but they are not claimed to be met.

While LLMs have transformed text generation, standard chat-and-canvas interfaces often reduce human authoring to quite passive supervision, causing review fatigue, over-reliance on AI, and the sidelining of the human role in long-form, source-grounded writing. Prior systems typically address isolated writing phases, leaving comprehensive end-to-end human-LLM collaboration largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce CoWriter, a proactive agentic scheme that adapts expert human (co-)authoring methodologies from cognitive science to flexibly steer the entire writing workflow while actively encouraging the user to engage. In an exploratory user study, compared to a standard LLM baseline, authors using CoWriter better expressed their perspectives and maintained a higher sense of document ownership, supported quantitatively by $2.2\times$ more successful agent engagements. Furthermore, external reader judges rated the resulting texts higher in "human touch" qualities like storytelling and integrating unique personal experiences. Overall, our results demonstrate that proactively engaging users through established human practices is beneficial for effective LLM-supported co-authoring, providing useful methodologies, techniques and insights for future research on collaborative agents.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping cybersecurity, moving it from signature-based reactive security to agentic, self-evolving, and proactive operations. However, the fast deployment of autonomous agents entails significant security issues, physical-layer attacks in cyber-physical systems, alignment problems, and advanced social engineering risks jeopardizing the stability of the modern sociotechnical infrastructures. This survey paper, which summarizes and analyses the literature, examines the duality of AI in cybersecurity, exploring its implications for strengthening digital defences and increasing the threat landscape for adversaries. We perform a thorough review of 36 cutting-edge research articles, which are organized into six important areas: self-evolving defensive paradigms, LLM-based intelligent agents, reinforcement learning for autonomous decision-making, security of cyber-physical systems, human-machine co-teaming, and agent alignment. Our synthesis shows that multi-agent collaborations greatly shorten incident response times and automate discovery of vulnerabilities but are also highly vulnerable to prompt injection, training data poisoning, and physical-layer spoofing. Moreover, we identify a shift from model patches to model alignment and constitutional safety at runtime as a prerequisite for securing these systems. We believe that resilient digital defence must also be considered a sociotechnical problem, as there must be agents, autonomous systems, that are governed by other agents, aligned and constitutionally bound, and are able to collaborate, rather than operate completely separately, with human operators.

Occupational exoskeletons promise significant reductions in worker physical burden and injury risk, yet industrial adoption rates remain low despite positive laboratory performance data. This persistent gap between demonstrated efficacy and actual deployment suggests that unmeasured barriers beyond task-performance metrics may influence adoption decisions. We examined whether pre- and post-use tasks generate usability problems that could act as barriers to adoption. Seven evaluators trained in human factors and heuristic evaluation evalauted three passive exoskeletons representing different support mechanisms: a shoulder-support device (Skelex), a lumbar-support device (Laevo), and a sit-stand support device (Chairless Chair). Using a combined framework of Nielsen usability heuristics and Shneiderman principles adapted for physical wearable systems, evaluators independently identified usability problems across all four deployment task phases, rated problem severity on a 5-point scale, and participated in structured reconciliation discussions to resolve rating divergences. Evaluators identified 158 usability problems across the three devices, 62 of which were rated as major problems (mean severity at or above 2.5): 29 for the shoulder-support, 15 for the back-support, and 18 for the sit-stand exoskeleton. Assembly accounted for 46% of the heuristic violations associated with major problems (114 of 250), ranging from 41% to 54% across devices. Agreement among the independent severity ratings was moderate for the seven-evaluator mean (ICC(2,7) = 0.67). Because the study did not measure adoption, these problems are plausible barriers to adoption that warrant field investigation. Six problem categories recurred across devices regardless of support mechanism, four of them in all three devices: two-person operation requirements (severity 2.9-3.1), poor documentation (severity 3.0), absent sequence indicators (severity 2.6-2.9), manual strength barriers (severity 2.7-3.1), universal design violations (severity 2.6–3.4), and hazards and safety problems, which included component ricochet on the shoulder-support device (severity 3.3–3.4), fall risk on the sit-stand device (severity 2.6–2.7), and pinch points on both. Based on our findings, we introduce three theoretical constructs extending heuristic evaluation theory to physical wearable systems: Deployment Ergonomics (encompassing physical, cognitive, temporal, and social demands of device preparation and removal), Visibility-Control Coupling (a design pattern where high force application and visual access requirements conflict), and the Assistance Paradox (the systemic contradiction whereby devices designed to reduce worker burden inadvertently create new demands, hazards, and barriers during setup). These constructs, derived from expert inspection and not yet validated in the field, offer a diagnostic framework for recurring design issues and a basis for design proposals.

documents.abstract: This paper develops a risk-based intellectual property (IP) governance framework for generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) through doctrinal, comparative, and normative analysis of the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom (UK), and the United States (US). It covers copyright and related IP challenges in data acquisition, model training, output creation, and commercial deployment, as well as the distribution of control, transparency, attribution, and liability in each jurisdiction. The analysis reveals that the EU has several text-and-data-mining exceptions and copyright-policy and training-content-summary obligations for general-purpose AI providers, while the UK has a very limited non-commercial research exception and a unique statutory exception for computer-generated works, and the US is driven primarily by the human-authorship doctrine and fact-specific fair-use analysis. While these strategies offer valuable protections, none alone establish a comprehensive system of organisational control. The study thus suggests an auditing framework linked to the legal basis, data provenance, licenses, human contribution to creativity, output testing, documentation, accountability and escalation, and periodic reassessment, according to the proportionate degree of risk. Rather than harmonizing the three legal systems, the framework sets out a common organizational process for identifying and managing differences in the three legal systems to safeguard the rights holders and to allow for responsible innovation.

The Internet and artificial intelligence (AI) have become deeply embedded in contemporary education, research and professional life. Their capacity to enhance learning efficiency and reduce access costs is undeniable. Yet these technologies have also generated significant negative externalities: students are increasingly distanced from printed textbooks and library-based study, turning instead to instantly available digital resources and generative AI tools. This shift has contributed to the erosion of deep reading, critical thinking and creativity. Drawing on recent empirical evidence, this article analyses the mechanisms through which screen-based reading and AI dependence undermine cognitive development, and argues that educational institutions must intervene through formal rules and regulations to minimise these externalities. It proposes a policy framework centred on the principle of preserving cognitive friction, encompassing curriculum design, pedagogical norms and assessment reform.
